def conditional(
    loc: Float[Array, " N"],
    cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    obs_idx: Int[Array, " M"],
    obs_values: Float[Array, " M"],
    *,
    solver: AbstractSolverStrategy | None = None,
) -> tuple[Float[Array, " R"], lx.AbstractLinearOperator]:
    """Conditional p(x_A ∣ x_B = b) of a joint Gaussian 𝒩(μ, Σ) from observed entries.

        μ_A|B = μ_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (b − μ_B)
        Σ_A|B = Σ_AA − Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA

    B holds the observed indices and A the remaining, free ones, in
    increasing order.

    Algorithm:
        1. Validate the observed indices B (on the host when concrete, with
           `equinox.error_if` when traced).
        2. Extract Σ_AA, Σ_AB and Σ_BB by structural dispatch, so structured
           operators (diagonal, block-diagonal) are not materialised whole.
        3. Solve Σ_BB⁻¹ (b − μ_B) and update the mean.
        4. Solve Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA with one factorisation, update the covariance
           and symmetrise it.

    Args:
        loc: Mean μ of the joint Gaussian.
        cov: Covariance Σ of the joint Gaussian.
        obs_idx: Observed indices B.
        obs_values: Observed values b of x_B.
        solver: Solver strategy for Σ_BB; ``None`` uses structural dispatch.

    Returns:
        Tuple ``(cond_mean, cond_cov)`` holding μ_A|B and Σ_A|B, the latter
        as a PSD-tagged `lineax.MatrixLinearOperator`.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``obs_idx`` is not 1D, does not match ``obs_values``
            in shape, or, when it is concrete, is out of bounds or contains
            duplicates.
        EquinoxRuntimeError: At run time, if a traced ``obs_idx`` is out of
            bounds or contains duplicates.

    Note:
        Usable under ``jax.jit``. Concrete indices (NumPy or JAX constants,
        including ones closed over by the jitted function) are validated
        on the host; traced indices are validated at run time with
        `equinox.error_if`, since an out-of-bounds gather would otherwise
        be silently clamped.

    Examples:
        Observe the second of two correlated entries:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> joint = jnp.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
        >>> covariance = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(joint, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
        >>> mean, cov = gaussx.conditional(
        ...     jnp.zeros(2), covariance, jnp.array([1]), jnp.array([1.0])
        ... )
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(mean, jnp.array([0.5])))
        True
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(cov.as_matrix(), jnp.array([[1.5]])))
        True

        Independent entries keep their prior block:

        >>> diagonal = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]))
        >>> mean, cov = gaussx.conditional(
        ...     jnp.ones(3), diagonal, jnp.array([0]), jnp.array([5.0])
        ... )
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(cov.as_matrix(), jnp.diag(jnp.array([2.0, 3.0]))))
        True

        Duplicate indices are rejected:

        >>> gaussx.conditional(
        ...     jnp.zeros(2), covariance, jnp.array([1, 1]), jnp.ones(2)
        ... )  # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        ValueError: obs_idx must not contain duplicates.
    """
    size = loc.shape[0]
    obs_values = jnp.asarray(obs_values, dtype=loc.dtype)

    if isinstance(obs_idx, Tracer):
        obs_idx = obs_idx.astype(jnp.int32)
        _check_shapes(obs_idx, obs_values)
        bad = jnp.any((obs_idx < 0) | (obs_idx >= size)) | jnp.any(
            jnp.diff(jnp.sort(obs_idx)) == 0
        )
        # Attached to obs_idx, which feeds both outputs, so the check cannot
        # be dead-code-eliminated when a caller uses only one of them.
        obs_idx = eqx.error_if(
            obs_idx,
            bad,
            f"obs_idx must be within bounds [0, {size}) and must not contain "
            "duplicates.",
        )
    else:
        # Cast before validating, so e.g. [1.1, 1.2] is caught as the
        # duplicate [1, 1] it becomes.
        idx_np = np.asarray(obs_idx).astype(np.int32)
        _check_shapes(idx_np, obs_values)
        if np.any((idx_np < 0) | (idx_np >= size)):
            raise ValueError(f"obs_idx must be within bounds [0, {size}).")
        if np.any(np.diff(np.sort(idx_np)) == 0):
            raise ValueError("obs_idx must not contain duplicates.")
        obs_idx = jnp.asarray(idx_np)

    # --- index sets ---
    # A, the complement of B, in increasing order
    free_mask = jnp.ones(size, dtype=bool).at[obs_idx].set(False)
    free_idx = jnp.where(free_mask, size=size - obs_idx.shape[0])[0]

    # --- blocks ---
    # Structural dispatch avoids materialising the whole joint Σ for
    # structured operators (Diagonal, BlockDiag); unstructured ones fall
    # back to full materialisation, where there is no cheaper alternative.
    # Σ_AA
    free_covariance = submatrix(cov, free_idx, free_idx)
    # Σ_AB
    cross_covariance = submatrix(cov, free_idx, obs_idx)
    # Σ_BB
    observed_covariance = submatrix(cov, obs_idx, obs_idx)
    # μ_A
    free_mean = loc[free_idx]
    # μ_B
    observed_mean = loc[obs_idx]

    # --- mean ---
    # b − μ_B
    residual = obs_values - observed_mean
    observed_covariance_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
        observed_covariance, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
    )
    # Σ_BB⁻¹ (b − μ_B)
    solved_residual = dispatch_solve(observed_covariance_op, residual, solver)
    # μ_A|B = μ_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (b − μ_B)
    cond_mean = free_mean + cross_covariance @ solved_residual

    # --- covariance ---
    # jnp, not einx: A or B may be empty here, and einx rejects a zero axis.
    # Σ_BA = Σ_ABᵀ
    cross_covariance_transpose = cross_covariance.T
    # Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA, one factorisation for every column in the PSD path
    solved_cross = solve_matrix(
        observed_covariance_op, cross_covariance_transpose, solver=solver
    )
    # jnp, not einx: A or B may be empty here, and einx rejects a zero axis.
    # Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA
    correction = cross_covariance @ solved_cross
    # Σ_A|B = Σ_AA − Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA
    cond_cov_matrix = free_covariance - correction
    # Round-off leaves Σ_A|B slightly asymmetric.
    cond_cov_matrix = symmetrize(cond_cov_matrix)
    cond_cov = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(cond_cov_matrix, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)

    return cond_mean, cond_cov

docs.title: linear_gaussian_update(prior_mean: Float[Array, '*state'], prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator, obs_operator: lx.AbstractLinearOperator, obs_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator, obs: Float[Array, '*obs'], *, solver: lx.AbstractLinearSolver | AbstractSolveStrategy | None = None) -> LinearGaussianPosterior
docs.text:
Matrix-free posterior of a linear-Gaussian observation.

S = H B Hᵀ + R,   G = B Hᵀ S⁻¹
x_a = x_b + G (y − H x_b)
P_a = (I − G H) B (I − G H)ᵀ + G R Gᵀ

This is the best linear unbiased estimate of Lorenc (1986), "Analysis methods for numerical weather prediction", Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 112, 1177-1194, doi:10.1002/qj.49711247414. P_a equals B − B Hᵀ S⁻¹ H B, but the Joseph form (gaussx.joseph_update) keeps its accuracy when R is small against H B Hᵀ, where the subtraction cancels. Each P_a matvec costs three B matvecs and two S solves, and B⁻¹ is never applied, so a smooth B that CG cannot invert is fine. For masked observations, pass a masked H and gaussx.masked_obs_covariance as R.

gaussx.kalman_gain and gaussx.schur_complement are the dense paths.

Algorithm
  1. Compose S = H B Hᵀ + R lazily, tagged positive semidefinite.
  2. Solve S v = y − H x_b, and set x_a = x_b + B Hᵀ v.
  3. Wrap P_a as a lazy operator in Joseph form, combining its two gain products into the two S solves per matvec.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default prior_mean Float[Array, '*state']

The prior mean x_b, in the shape B acts on.

required prior_cov AbstractLinearOperator

The prior covariance B, N × N.

required obs_operator AbstractLinearOperator

The linear observation operator H, M × N.

required obs_cov AbstractLinearOperator

The noise covariance R, M × M.

required obs Float[Array, '*obs']

The observation y, in the shape R acts on.

required solver AbstractLinearSolver | AbstractSolveStrategy | None

How to solve against S. Default None is gaussx.solve, which materialises S; pass gaussx.CGSolver to stay matrix-free.

None

Returns:

Type Description LinearGaussianPosterior

The posterior mean and lazy covariance. P_a is symmetric only up to

LinearGaussianPosterior

the tolerance of the S solve, and is tagged PSD regardless.

Examples:

One observed entry with unit prior and noise halves its variance:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> B = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(2))
>>> H = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0]]))
>>> R = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(1))
>>> posterior = gaussx.linear_gaussian_update(
...     jnp.zeros(2), B, H, R, jnp.array([1.0])
... )
>>> [round(float(v), 4) for v in posterior.mean]
[0.5, 0.0]
>>> [round(float(v), 4) for v in gaussx.diag(posterior.cov)]
[0.5, 1.0]

def linear_gaussian_update(
    prior_mean: Float[Array, "*state"],
    prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    obs_operator: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    obs_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    obs: Float[Array, "*obs"],
    *,
    solver: lx.AbstractLinearSolver | AbstractSolveStrategy | None = None,
) -> LinearGaussianPosterior:
    """Matrix-free posterior of a linear-Gaussian observation.

        S = H B Hᵀ + R,   G = B Hᵀ S⁻¹
        x_a = x_b + G (y − H x_b)
        P_a = (I − G H) B (I − G H)ᵀ + G R Gᵀ

    This is the best linear unbiased estimate of Lorenc (1986), "Analysis
    methods for numerical weather prediction", *Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc.* 112,
    1177-1194, doi:10.1002/qj.49711247414. P_a equals B − B Hᵀ S⁻¹ H B, but
    the Joseph form (`gaussx.joseph_update`) keeps its accuracy when R is small
    against H B Hᵀ, where the subtraction cancels. Each P_a matvec costs three
    B matvecs and two S solves, and B⁻¹ is never applied, so a smooth B that
    CG cannot invert is fine. For masked observations, pass a masked H and
    `gaussx.masked_obs_covariance` as R.

    `gaussx.kalman_gain` and `gaussx.schur_complement` are the dense paths.

    Algorithm:
        1. Compose S = H B Hᵀ + R lazily, tagged positive semidefinite.
        2. Solve S v = y − H x_b, and set x_a = x_b + B Hᵀ v.
        3. Wrap P_a as a lazy operator in Joseph form, combining its two
           gain products into the two S solves per matvec.

    Args:
        prior_mean: The prior mean x_b, in the shape B acts on.
        prior_cov: The prior covariance B, N × N.
        obs_operator: The linear observation operator H, M × N.
        obs_cov: The noise covariance R, M × M.
        obs: The observation y, in the shape R acts on.
        solver: How to solve against S. Default ``None`` is `gaussx.solve`,
            which materialises S; pass `gaussx.CGSolver` to stay matrix-free.

    Returns:
        The posterior mean and lazy covariance. P_a is symmetric only up to
        the tolerance of the S solve, and is tagged PSD regardless.

    Examples:
        One observed entry with unit prior and noise halves its variance:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> B = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(2))
        >>> H = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0]]))
        >>> R = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(1))
        >>> posterior = gaussx.linear_gaussian_update(
        ...     jnp.zeros(2), B, H, R, jnp.array([1.0])
        ... )
        >>> [round(float(v), 4) for v in posterior.mean]
        [0.5, 0.0]
        >>> [round(float(v), 4) for v in gaussx.diag(posterior.cov)]
        [0.5, 1.0]
    """
    adjoint = obs_operator.T
    # S = H B Hᵀ + R
    innovation_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(
        obs_operator @ prior_cov @ adjoint + obs_cov, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
    )
    # d = y − H x_b
    innovation = obs - obs_operator.mv(prior_mean)
    # v = S⁻¹ d
    weights = dispatch_solve(innovation_cov, innovation, solver)
    # x_a = x_b + B Hᵀ v
    mean = prior_mean + prior_cov.mv(adjoint.mv(weights))

    def posterior_mv(direction: Float[Array, "*state"]) -> Float[Array, "*state"]:
        # Gᵀ v = S⁻¹ H B v
        gain_adjoint = dispatch_solve(
            innovation_cov, obs_operator.mv(prior_cov.mv(direction)), solver
        )
        # B (I − G H)ᵀ v = B (v − Hᵀ Gᵀ v)
        joseph_direction = prior_cov.mv(direction - adjoint.mv(gain_adjoint))
        # S⁻¹ (R Gᵀ v − H B (I − G H)ᵀ v)
        correction = dispatch_solve(
            innovation_cov,
            obs_cov.mv(gain_adjoint) - obs_operator.mv(joseph_direction),
            solver,
        )
        # (I − G H) B (I − G H)ᵀ v + G R Gᵀ v
        return joseph_direction + prior_cov.mv(adjoint.mv(correction))

    cov = as_linear_operator(
        posterior_mv,
        in_structure=prior_cov.in_structure(),
        positive_semidefinite=True,
    )
    return LinearGaussianPosterior(mean=mean, cov=cov)

docs.text:
Averaging kernel, DOFS and information content of a linear retrieval.

Ŝ⁻¹ = Kᵀ S_ε⁻¹ K + S_a⁻¹
A = Ŝ Kᵀ S_ε⁻¹ K
d_s = tr A
H = ½ (ln det S_a + ln det Ŝ⁻¹)
S_m = A Ŝ

H is the mutual information between the state and the measurement, and 0 ≤ d_s ≤ min(n, m). See Rodgers (2000), Inverse Methods for Atmospheric Sounding: Theory and Practice, World Scientific, doi:10.1142/3171, chapters 2 and 3.

Algorithm
  1. Whiten with structured factors, K̃ = L_ε⁻¹ K and L_a⁻¹, where L_ε L_εᵀ = S_ε and L_a L_aᵀ = S_a, so neither covariance is materialised beyond the n × n outputs.
  2. Factor the stacked [K̃; L_a⁻¹] = [Q_K; Q_a] T by QR, so Ŝ⁻¹ = Tᵀ T without forming K̃ᵀ K̃, which would round away the prior when K̃ is large.
  3. Read the diagnostics off the factors: Ŝ = T⁻¹ T⁻ᵀ, A = T⁻¹ Q_Kᵀ K̃, since K̃ T⁻¹ = Q_K, and ln det Ŝ⁻¹ = 2 ∑ᵢ ln |T_ii|.

A gaussx.SparseOperator covariance is materialised, with a warning: its Cholesky factor solves against the whole covariance and offers no whitening by its root.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default jacobian Float[Array, 'm n']

The Jacobian K of the forward model at the retrieval.

required noise_cov AbstractLinearOperator

The measurement-noise covariance S_ε, m × m.

required prior_cov AbstractLinearOperator

The prior covariance S_a, n × n.

required

Returns:

Type Description InformationDiagnostics

The five diagnostics, as dense arrays.

Examples:

One unit measurement of one state with a unit prior carries half a degree of freedom and ½ ln 2 nats:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> identity = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(1))
>>> diagnostics = gaussx.information_diagnostics(
...     jnp.ones((1, 1)), identity, identity
... )
>>> round(float(diagnostics.dofs), 4)
0.5
>>> round(float(diagnostics.information_content), 4)
0.3466
>>> round(float(diagnostics.retrieval_noise_cov[0, 0]), 4)
0.25

def information_diagnostics(
    jacobian: Float[Array, "m n"],
    noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
) -> InformationDiagnostics:
    """Averaging kernel, DOFS and information content of a linear retrieval.

        Ŝ⁻¹ = Kᵀ S_ε⁻¹ K + S_a⁻¹
        A = Ŝ Kᵀ S_ε⁻¹ K
        d_s = tr A
        H = ½ (ln det S_a + ln det Ŝ⁻¹)
        S_m = A Ŝ

    H is the mutual information between the state and the measurement, and
    0 ≤ d_s ≤ min(n, m). See Rodgers (2000), *Inverse Methods for Atmospheric
    Sounding: Theory and Practice*, World Scientific, doi:10.1142/3171,
    chapters 2 and 3.

    Algorithm:
        1. Whiten with structured factors, K̃ = L_ε⁻¹ K and L_a⁻¹, where
           L_ε L_εᵀ = S_ε and L_a L_aᵀ = S_a, so neither covariance is
           materialised beyond the n × n outputs.
        2. Factor the stacked [K̃; L_a⁻¹] = [Q_K; Q_a] T by QR, so
           Ŝ⁻¹ = Tᵀ T without forming K̃ᵀ K̃, which would round away the prior
           when K̃ is large.
        3. Read the diagnostics off the factors: Ŝ = T⁻¹ T⁻ᵀ,
           A = T⁻¹ Q_Kᵀ K̃, since K̃ T⁻¹ = Q_K, and
           ln det Ŝ⁻¹ = 2 ∑ᵢ ln |T_ii|.

    A `gaussx.SparseOperator` covariance is materialised, with a warning: its
    Cholesky factor solves against the whole covariance and offers no whitening
    by its root.

    Args:
        jacobian: The Jacobian K of the forward model at the retrieval.
        noise_cov: The measurement-noise covariance S_ε, m × m.
        prior_cov: The prior covariance S_a, n × n.

    Returns:
        The five diagnostics, as dense arrays.

    Examples:
        One unit measurement of one state with a unit prior carries half a
        degree of freedom and ½ ln 2 nats:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> identity = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(1))
        >>> diagnostics = gaussx.information_diagnostics(
        ...     jnp.ones((1, 1)), identity, identity
        ... )
        >>> round(float(diagnostics.dofs), 4)
        0.5
        >>> round(float(diagnostics.information_content), 4)
        0.3466
        >>> round(float(diagnostics.retrieval_noise_cov[0, 0]), 4)
        0.25
    """
    n_state = jacobian.shape[1]
    identity = jnp.eye(n_state, dtype=jacobian.dtype)
    # K̃ = L_ε⁻¹ K
    whitened_jacobian = solve_columns(_whitening_root(noise_cov), jacobian)
    # L_a⁻¹
    prior_root_inverse = solve_columns(_whitening_root(prior_cov), identity)
    # [K̃; L_a⁻¹] = [Q_K; Q_a] T, so Ŝ⁻¹ = Tᵀ T
    orthogonal, triangular = jnp.linalg.qr(
        jnp.vstack([whitened_jacobian, prior_root_inverse])
    )
    # T⁻¹
    triangular_inverse = jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(
        triangular, identity, lower=False
    )
    # Ŝ = T⁻¹ T⁻ᵀ
    posterior_cov = symmetrize(
        einsum(triangular_inverse, triangular_inverse, "i k, j k -> i j")
    )
    # K̃ T⁻¹ = Q_K, the observation rows of Q; multiplying K̃ by T⁻¹ would cancel
    gain_factor = orthogonal[: jacobian.shape[0]]
    # A = Ŝ K̃ᵀ K̃ = T⁻¹ Q_Kᵀ K̃
    averaging_kernel = einsum(
        triangular_inverse, gain_factor, whitened_jacobian, "i k, m k, m j -> i j"
    )
    # S_m = A Ŝ
    retrieval_noise_cov = symmetrize(
        einsum(averaging_kernel, posterior_cov, "i k, k j -> i j")
    )
    # ln det Ŝ⁻¹ = 2 ∑ᵢ ln |T_ii|
    logdet_precision = 2.0 * jnp.sum(jnp.log(jnp.abs(jnp.diag(triangular))))
    return InformationDiagnostics(
        averaging_kernel=averaging_kernel,
        # d_s = tr A
        dofs=jnp.trace(averaging_kernel),
        # H = ½ (ln det S_a + ln det Ŝ⁻¹)
        information_content=0.5 * (logdet(prior_cov) + logdet_precision),
        posterior_cov=posterior_cov,
        retrieval_noise_cov=retrieval_noise_cov,
    )

docs.title: joseph_update(P_pred: Float[Array, 'N N'], K: Float[Array, 'N M'], H: Float[Array, 'M N'], R: Float[Array, 'M M']) -> Float[Array, 'N N']
docs.text:
Joseph-form posterior covariance of a Kalman update, stable for any gain.

Σ_x|y = (I − G H) Σ_x (I − G H)ᵀ + G Σ_ε Gᵀ

For the optimal gain G = Σ_x Hᵀ Σ_y⁻¹ this equals Σ_x − G Σ_y Gᵀ, but the Joseph form stays symmetric positive semi-definite when G is approximate or the problem is poorly conditioned, where the short forms Σ_x − G Σ_y Gᵀ and (I − G H) Σ_x can lose definiteness.

Algorithm
  1. Form I − G H.
  2. Sandwich the prior covariance, (I − G H) Σ_x (I − G H)ᵀ.
  3. Add the noise term G Σ_ε Gᵀ and symmetrise.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default P_pred Float[Array, 'N N']

Prior (predicted) covariance Σ_x of the state.

required K Float[Array, 'N M']

Kalman gain G.

required H Float[Array, 'M N']

Observation operator H.

required R Float[Array, 'M M']

Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.

required

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, 'N N']

The posterior covariance Σ_x|y, symmetrised.

Examples:

With the optimal gain it matches Σ_x − G Σ_y Gᵀ:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> prior_covariance = jnp.eye(2)
>>> obs_operator = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0]])
>>> obs_noise_covariance = jnp.array([[1.0]])
>>> gain = gaussx.kalman_gain(
...     lx.MatrixLinearOperator(prior_covariance),
...     lx.MatrixLinearOperator(obs_operator),
...     lx.MatrixLinearOperator(obs_noise_covariance),
... )
>>> posterior = gaussx.joseph_update(
...     prior_covariance, gain, obs_operator, obs_noise_covariance
... )
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(posterior, jnp.diag(jnp.array([0.5, 1.0]))))
True

A suboptimal gain still gives a symmetric covariance:

>>> suboptimal = jnp.array([[0.3], [0.1]])
>>> posterior = gaussx.joseph_update(
...     prior_covariance, suboptimal, obs_operator, obs_noise_covariance
... )
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(posterior, posterior.T))
True
Source code in src/gaussx/_distributions/_joseph.py 
def joseph_update(
    P_pred: Float[Array, "N N"],
    K: Float[Array, "N M"],
    H: Float[Array, "M N"],
    R: Float[Array, "M M"],
) -> Float[Array, "N N"]:
    """Joseph-form posterior covariance of a Kalman update, stable for any gain.

        Σ_x|y = (I − G H) Σ_x (I − G H)ᵀ + G Σ_ε Gᵀ

    For the optimal gain G = Σ_x Hᵀ Σ_y⁻¹ this equals Σ_x − G Σ_y Gᵀ, but
    the Joseph form stays symmetric positive semi-definite when G is
    approximate or the problem is poorly conditioned, where the short forms
    Σ_x − G Σ_y Gᵀ and (I − G H) Σ_x can lose definiteness.

    Algorithm:
        1. Form I − G H.
        2. Sandwich the prior covariance, (I − G H) Σ_x (I − G H)ᵀ.
        3. Add the noise term G Σ_ε Gᵀ and symmetrise.

    Args:
        P_pred: Prior (predicted) covariance Σ_x of the state.
        K: Kalman gain G.
        H: Observation operator H.
        R: Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.

    Returns:
        The posterior covariance Σ_x|y, symmetrised.

    Examples:
        With the optimal gain it matches Σ_x − G Σ_y Gᵀ:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> prior_covariance = jnp.eye(2)
        >>> obs_operator = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0]])
        >>> obs_noise_covariance = jnp.array([[1.0]])
        >>> gain = gaussx.kalman_gain(
        ...     lx.MatrixLinearOperator(prior_covariance),
        ...     lx.MatrixLinearOperator(obs_operator),
        ...     lx.MatrixLinearOperator(obs_noise_covariance),
        ... )
        >>> posterior = gaussx.joseph_update(
        ...     prior_covariance, gain, obs_operator, obs_noise_covariance
        ... )
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(posterior, jnp.diag(jnp.array([0.5, 1.0]))))
        True

        A suboptimal gain still gives a symmetric covariance:

        >>> suboptimal = jnp.array([[0.3], [0.1]])
        >>> posterior = gaussx.joseph_update(
        ...     prior_covariance, suboptimal, obs_operator, obs_noise_covariance
        ... )
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(posterior, posterior.T))
        True
    """
    state_size = P_pred.shape[0]
    # jnp, not einx: einx rejects a zero-length axis, and D_x = 0 or D_y = 0
    # is accepted here.
    identity = jnp.eye(state_size, dtype=P_pred.dtype)
    # G H
    gain_obs_operator = K @ H
    # I − G H
    joseph_factor = identity - gain_obs_operator
    # (I − G H) Σ_x
    factor_covariance = joseph_factor @ P_pred
    # (I − G H) Σ_x (I − G H)ᵀ
    propagated = factor_covariance @ joseph_factor.T
    # G Σ_ε
    gain_noise = K @ R
    # G Σ_ε Gᵀ
    noise_term = gain_noise @ K.T
    # Σ_x|y = (I − G H) Σ_x (I − G H)ᵀ + G Σ_ε Gᵀ
    posterior_covariance = propagated + noise_term
    # ½ (Σ_x|y + Σ_x|yᵀ)
    return symmetrize(posterior_covariance)

Diagonal jitter A + β I for numerical stability.

Examples:

Jitter a singular matrix:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> singular = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.ones((2, 2)))
>>> jittered = gaussx.add_jitter(singular, jitter=0.5)
>>> expected = jnp.ones((2, 2)) + 0.5 * jnp.eye(2)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(jittered.as_matrix(), expected))
True

The jitter takes the operator's dtype:

>>> single = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(2, dtype=jnp.float32))
>>> gaussx.add_jitter(single).as_matrix().dtype
dtype('float32')
Source code in src/gaussx/_distributions/_gaussian.py 
def add_jitter(
    operator: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    jitter: float = 1e-6,
) -> lx.AbstractLinearOperator:
    """Diagonal jitter A + β I for numerical stability.

        A + β I

    Args:
        operator: Square operator A.
        jitter: Jitter β added to every diagonal entry. Default ``1e-6``.

    Returns:
        A + β I as a lineax ``AddLinearOperator``, in the dtype of A.

    Examples:
        Jitter a singular matrix:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> singular = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.ones((2, 2)))
        >>> jittered = gaussx.add_jitter(singular, jitter=0.5)
        >>> expected = jnp.ones((2, 2)) + 0.5 * jnp.eye(2)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(jittered.as_matrix(), expected))
        True

        The jitter takes the operator's dtype:

        >>> single = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(2, dtype=jnp.float32))
        >>> gaussx.add_jitter(single).as_matrix().dtype
        dtype('float32')
    """
    size = operator.in_size()
    dtype = operator.out_structure().dtype
    # β I, in the dtype of A
    jitter_operator = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.full(size, jitter, dtype=dtype))
    # A + β I
    return operator + jitter_operator

docs.title: project(K_XZ: Float[Array, 'B M'], L_Z: lx.AbstractLinearOperator) -> Float[Array, 'B M']
docs.text:
Projection A_X = K_Xℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹ onto the inducing inputs via Cholesky solves.

A_X = K_Xℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹,   K_ℐℐ = L_ℐℐ L_ℐℐᵀ

Used in sparse variational GPs to project test inputs onto the inducing space. Row n of A_X is (K_ℐℐ⁻¹ k_ℐn)ᵀ.

Algorithm
  1. Tag L_ℐℐ lower-triangular if it is not already.
  2. For each input n, solve L_ℐℐ v_n = k_ℐn by forward substitution.
  3. Solve L_ℐℐᵀ a_n = v_n by back substitution; a_n is row n of A_X.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default K_XZ Float[Array, 'B M']

Kernel matrix K_Xℐ between the inputs and the inducing inputs.

required L_Z AbstractLinearOperator

Lower Cholesky factor L_ℐℐ of K_ℐℐ. It need not carry lineax.lower_triangular_tag: the tag is added when missing (the factor is lower-triangular by precondition), and L_Z.T is then upper-triangular.

required

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, 'B M']

The projection A_X, one row per input.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If L_Z is not N_ℐ × N_ℐ with N_ℐ the number of columns of K_XZ.

Examples:

A diagonal inducing kernel matrix K_ℐℐ = 4 I:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> factor = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
...     2.0 * jnp.eye(2), lx.lower_triangular_tag
... )
>>> cross = jnp.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 4.0]])
>>> projection = gaussx.project(cross, factor)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(projection, jnp.array([[0.5, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])))
True

An untagged factor from jnp.linalg.cholesky matches a dense solve:

>>> inducing = jnp.array([[2.0, 0.5], [0.5, 1.0]])
>>> untagged = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.linalg.cholesky(inducing))
>>> cross = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.2], [0.3, 0.7], [0.0, 1.0]])
>>> projection = gaussx.project(cross, untagged)
>>> projection.shape
(3, 2)
>>> expected = jnp.linalg.solve(inducing, cross.T).T
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(projection, expected, atol=1e-5))
True

A factor of the wrong size is rejected:

>>> wide = jnp.ones((2, 3))
>>> gaussx.project(wide, factor)

def project(
    K_XZ: Float[Array, "B M"],
    L_Z: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
) -> Float[Array, "B M"]:
    """Projection A_X = K_Xℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹ onto the inducing inputs via Cholesky solves.

        A_X = K_Xℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹,   K_ℐℐ = L_ℐℐ L_ℐℐᵀ

    Used in sparse variational GPs to project test inputs onto the
    inducing space. Row n of A_X is (K_ℐℐ⁻¹ k_ℐn)ᵀ.

    Algorithm:
        1. Tag L_ℐℐ lower-triangular if it is not already.
        2. For each input n, solve L_ℐℐ v_n = k_ℐn by forward substitution.
        3. Solve L_ℐℐᵀ a_n = v_n by back substitution; a_n is row n of A_X.

    Args:
        K_XZ: Kernel matrix K_Xℐ between the inputs and the inducing inputs.
        L_Z: Lower Cholesky factor L_ℐℐ of K_ℐℐ. It need not carry
            ``lineax.lower_triangular_tag``: the tag is added when missing
            (the factor is lower-triangular by precondition), and
            ``L_Z.T`` is then upper-triangular.

    Returns:
        The projection A_X, one row per input.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``L_Z`` is not N_ℐ × N_ℐ with N_ℐ the number of
            columns of ``K_XZ``.

    Examples:
        A diagonal inducing kernel matrix K_ℐℐ = 4 I:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> factor = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
        ...     2.0 * jnp.eye(2), lx.lower_triangular_tag
        ... )
        >>> cross = jnp.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 4.0]])
        >>> projection = gaussx.project(cross, factor)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(projection, jnp.array([[0.5, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])))
        True

        An untagged factor from ``jnp.linalg.cholesky`` matches a dense solve:

        >>> inducing = jnp.array([[2.0, 0.5], [0.5, 1.0]])
        >>> untagged = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.linalg.cholesky(inducing))
        >>> cross = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.2], [0.3, 0.7], [0.0, 1.0]])
        >>> projection = gaussx.project(cross, untagged)
        >>> projection.shape
        (3, 2)
        >>> expected = jnp.linalg.solve(inducing, cross.T).T
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(projection, expected, atol=1e-5))
        True

        A factor of the wrong size is rejected:

        >>> wide = jnp.ones((2, 3))
        >>> gaussx.project(wide, factor)  # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        ValueError: L_Z must be (3, 3) to match K_XZ's 3 columns, got (2, 2).
    """
    inducing_size = K_XZ.shape[-1]
    if L_Z.in_size() != inducing_size or L_Z.out_size() != inducing_size:
        raise ValueError(
            f"L_Z must be ({inducing_size}, {inducing_size}) to match K_XZ's "
            f"{inducing_size} columns, got ({L_Z.out_size()}, {L_Z.in_size()})."
        )
    if not lx.is_lower_triangular(L_Z):
        # lx.Triangular checks tags, so an untagged factor (e.g. built from
        # jnp.linalg.cholesky) would be rejected.
        L_Z = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(L_Z, lx.lower_triangular_tag)
    solver = lx.Triangular()

    def _solve_row(kernel_column):
        # v_n = L_ℐℐ⁻¹ k_ℐn
        forward = lx.linear_solve(L_Z, kernel_column, solver).value
        # a_n = L_ℐℐ⁻ᵀ v_n = K_ℐℐ⁻¹ k_ℐn
        return lx.linear_solve(L_Z.T, forward, solver).value

    # A_X, one row a_nᵀ per input
    return jax.vmap(_solve_row)(K_XZ)

docs.title: Structured sampling
docs.text:
sample_mvn draws \(\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{L} \mathbf{z}\) with \(\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\) and \(\mathbf{L} \mathbf{L}^\top = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), picking the factor \(\mathbf{L}\) from the structure of the covariance operator: element-wise for a diagonal, per factor for a Kronecker product, per block for a block-diagonal, FFT circulant embedding for a Toeplitz, and \(\mathbf{L}_{\mathbf{A}_0} \mathbf{z}_1 + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{D}^{1/2} \mathbf{z}_2\) for a low-rank update \(\mathbf{A}_0 + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{D} \mathbf{U}^\top\), so a \(10^4 \times 10^4\) Kronecker covariance is never factorised densely. Every branch is exact. A SumOfKroneckers therefore takes the dense symmetric square root: its matrix-free sampler, sum_of_kroneckers_sample, is a truncated Lanczos approximation and stays an explicit opt-in. The one-off helpers toeplitz_sample and kronecker_sum_sample also remain available for callers that want them directly.

sample_joint_conditional draws a partitioned Gaussian \((\mathbf{x}_A, \mathbf{x}_B)\) jointly without forming its \((N + M)^2\) covariance: the observed block \(B\) through sample_mvn, so it keeps its structure, and the other, \(A\), through the gain \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{AB} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{BB}^{-1}\) plus a square root of the Schur complement. Given an observed value it also returns conditional draws that share the same noise, which makes them exactly the matheron_update of the joint draws.

Structured linear algebra and Gaussian primitives for JAX.

docs.title: sample_mvn(mean: Float[Array, '*batch N'], covariance: lx.AbstractLinearOperator, *, key: jax.Array, num_samples: int = 1) -> Float[Array, 'num_samples *batch N']
docs.text:
Draw samples from 𝒩(μ, Σ), dispatching on the structure of Σ.

x = μ + L z,   z ~ 𝒩(0, I),   L Lᵀ = Σ

Every branch draws x exactly (no branch approximates the covariance), and only the factor L changes:

Covariance Σ Factor Cost lineax.DiagonalLinearOperator σ ⊙ z O(D_x) gaussx.BlockDiag each block by its own rule per block gaussx.Kronecker per-factor eigendecomposition O(N_1³ + … + N_D³) gaussx.KroneckerSum per-factor eigendecomposition O(N_1³ + N_2³) gaussx.BlockTriDiag block-banded Cholesky O(B d³) gaussx.Toeplitz FFT circulant embedding O(D_x log D_x) gaussx.LowRankUpdate L_A₀ z₁ + U D^½ z₂ A₀'s cost + O(D_x k) anything else dense symmetric square root Σ^½ O(D_x³)

Here a diagonal is Σ = diag(σ²); a Kronecker product A_1 ⊗ … ⊗ A_D has factors of sizes N_1, …, N_D and a Kronecker sum A_1 ⊕ A_2 two; a block-tridiagonal Σ has B diagonal blocks of size d; and a low-rank update A₀ + U D Uᵀ has rank k and L_A₀ L_A₀ᵀ = A₀.

lineax.TaggedLinearOperator wrappers are looked through, and a scalar multiple c Σ (with c > 0) samples Σ and rescales by √c, so wrapping never costs the structure underneath.

The Kronecker branches work in the factors' eigenbases, where the eigenvalues of the whole operator are products (or sums) of the factors' ones. That keeps them exact when a factor is indefinite but the product is not, as in (−A_1) ⊗ (−A_2), and when the covariance is only semi-definite. The dense fallback is the symmetric square root for the same reason: a Cholesky factor of a singular covariance is NaN.

A gaussx.SumOfKroneckers takes the dense fallback: its matrix-free square root, gaussx.sum_of_kroneckers_sample, is a truncated Lanczos approximation, so it stays an explicit opt-in rather than a default.

Some structured routes hold only for some values, and each takes the dense square root otherwise, so every covariance the operator can represent is sampled exactly and pathwise gradients stay finite:

  • a scalar multiple c Σ needs c > 0;
  • a gaussx.Toeplitz needs a circulant embedding (2, 4, 8 or 16 times D_x) whose spectrum is strictly positive: a zero eigenvalue there would put √0 in the pathwise derivative;
  • a gaussx.LowRankUpdate A₀ + U D Vᵀ needs V = U established (the same array, or equal values), a base A₀ that is a covariance in its own right (tagged positive semi-definite, or a strictly positive diagonal), and every weight in D positive: a zero weight would again put √0 in the derivative.

When those values are only known at run time (under jax.jit), the choice is a jax.lax.cond, which runs only the branch it takes; under jax.vmap it evaluates both.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mean Float[Array, '*batch N']

Mean μ, with leading batch axes. Each batch element gets independent noise; the covariance is shared.

required covariance AbstractLinearOperator

Positive-definite covariance Σ, D_x × D_x.

required key Array

PRNG key.

required num_samples int

Number of independent draws.

1

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, 'num_samples *batch N']

Samples x of shape (num_samples, *batch, N).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If covariance is not square, does not match the last axis of mean, or num_samples is below one.

Examples:

Five draws from a diagonal covariance:

>>> import jax
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> covariance = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.array([1.0, 4.0, 9.0]))
>>> samples = gaussx.sample_mvn(
...     jnp.zeros(3), covariance, key=jax.random.key(0), num_samples=5
... )
>>> samples.shape
(5, 3)

A batch of means shares the covariance:

>>> means = jnp.zeros((4, 3))
>>> batch = gaussx.sample_mvn(
...     means, covariance, key=jax.random.key(1), num_samples=2
... )
>>> batch.shape
(2, 4, 3)

A zero covariance returns the mean:

>>> zero = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.zeros(3))
>>> mean = jnp.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
>>> draws = gaussx.sample_mvn(mean, zero, key=jax.random.key(2))
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(draws, mean))
True

def sample_mvn(
    mean: Float[Array, "*batch N"],
    covariance: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    *,
    key: jax.Array,
    num_samples: int = 1,
) -> Float[Array, "num_samples *batch N"]:
    """Draw samples from 𝒩(μ, Σ), dispatching on the structure of Σ.

        x = μ + L z,   z ~ 𝒩(0, I),   L Lᵀ = Σ

    Every branch draws x *exactly* (no branch approximates the covariance),
    and only the factor L changes:

    | Covariance Σ | Factor | Cost |
    |---|---|---|
    | `lineax.DiagonalLinearOperator` | σ ⊙ z | O(D_x) |
    | `gaussx.BlockDiag` | each block by its own rule | per block |
    | `gaussx.Kronecker` | per-factor eigendecomposition | O(N_1³ + … + N_D³) |
    | `gaussx.KroneckerSum` | per-factor eigendecomposition | O(N_1³ + N_2³) |
    | `gaussx.BlockTriDiag` | block-banded Cholesky | O(B d³) |
    | `gaussx.Toeplitz` | FFT circulant embedding | O(D_x log D_x) |
    | `gaussx.LowRankUpdate` | L_A₀ z₁ + U D^½ z₂ | A₀'s cost + O(D_x k) |
    | anything else | dense symmetric square root Σ^½ | O(D_x³) |

    Here a diagonal is Σ = diag(σ²); a Kronecker product A_1 ⊗ … ⊗ A_D has
    factors of sizes N_1, …, N_D and a Kronecker sum A_1 ⊕ A_2 two; a
    block-tridiagonal Σ has B diagonal blocks of size d; and a low-rank
    update A₀ + U D Uᵀ has rank k and L_A₀ L_A₀ᵀ = A₀.

    `lineax.TaggedLinearOperator` wrappers are looked through, and a scalar
    multiple c Σ (with c > 0) samples Σ and rescales by √c, so wrapping
    never costs the structure underneath.

    The Kronecker branches work in the factors' eigenbases, where the
    eigenvalues of the whole operator are products (or sums) of the
    factors' ones. That keeps them exact when a factor is indefinite but
    the product is not, as in (−A_1) ⊗ (−A_2), and when the covariance is
    only semi-definite. The dense fallback is the symmetric square root for
    the same reason: a Cholesky factor of a singular covariance is ``NaN``.

    A `gaussx.SumOfKroneckers` takes the dense fallback: its matrix-free
    square root, `gaussx.sum_of_kroneckers_sample`, is a truncated Lanczos
    approximation, so it stays an explicit opt-in rather than a default.

    Some structured routes hold only for some values, and each takes the
    dense square root otherwise, so every covariance the operator can
    represent is sampled exactly and pathwise gradients stay finite:

    - a scalar multiple c Σ needs c > 0;
    - a `gaussx.Toeplitz` needs a circulant embedding (2, 4, 8 or 16 times
      D_x) whose spectrum is strictly positive: a zero eigenvalue there
      would put √0 in the pathwise derivative;
    - a `gaussx.LowRankUpdate` A₀ + U D Vᵀ needs V = U established (the
      same array, or equal values), a base A₀ that is a covariance in its
      own right (tagged positive semi-definite, or a strictly positive
      diagonal), and every weight in D positive: a zero weight would again
      put √0 in the derivative.

    When those values are only known at run time (under `jax.jit`), the
    choice is a `jax.lax.cond`, which runs only the branch it takes; under
    `jax.vmap` it evaluates both.

    Args:
        mean: Mean μ, with leading batch axes. Each batch element gets
            independent noise; the covariance is shared.
        covariance: Positive-definite covariance Σ, D_x × D_x.
        key: PRNG key.
        num_samples: Number of independent draws.

    Returns:
        Samples x of shape ``(num_samples, *batch, N)``.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``covariance`` is not square, does not match the last
            axis of ``mean``, or ``num_samples`` is below one.

    Examples:
        Five draws from a diagonal covariance:

        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> covariance = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.array([1.0, 4.0, 9.0]))
        >>> samples = gaussx.sample_mvn(
        ...     jnp.zeros(3), covariance, key=jax.random.key(0), num_samples=5
        ... )
        >>> samples.shape
        (5, 3)

        A batch of means shares the covariance:

        >>> means = jnp.zeros((4, 3))
        >>> batch = gaussx.sample_mvn(
        ...     means, covariance, key=jax.random.key(1), num_samples=2
        ... )
        >>> batch.shape
        (2, 4, 3)

        A zero covariance returns the mean:

        >>> zero = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.zeros(3))
        >>> mean = jnp.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
        >>> draws = gaussx.sample_mvn(mean, zero, key=jax.random.key(2))
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(draws, mean))
        True
    """
    mean = jnp.asarray(mean)
    if covariance.in_size() != covariance.out_size():
        raise ValueError(
            "sample_mvn requires a square covariance, got "
            f"{covariance.out_size()}x{covariance.in_size()}."
        )
    if mean.ndim < 1 or mean.shape[-1] != covariance.in_size():
        raise ValueError(
            f"mean must have shape (*batch, {covariance.in_size()}), got {mean.shape}."
        )
    if num_samples < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"num_samples must be at least 1, got {num_samples}.")

    batch_shape = mean.shape[:-1]
    num_draws = num_samples * math.prod(batch_shape)
    if num_draws == 0:
        # An empty batch: nothing to draw, but the output keeps its shape.
        # The represented dtype, which `in_structure` can understate (a
        # LowRankUpdate reports its base's). Abstract, so nothing is formed.
        matrix_dtype = jax.eval_shape(covariance.as_matrix).dtype
        dtype = jnp.result_type(mean, matrix_dtype)
        return jnp.zeros((num_samples, *mean.shape), dtype=dtype)
    # L z, one row per draw
    draws = _zero_mean_draws(covariance, key, num_draws)

    batch_axes = [f"b{index}" for index in range(len(batch_shape))]
    batch_pattern = " ".join(batch_axes)
    pattern = f"(s {batch_pattern}) n -> s {batch_pattern} n"
    batch_sizes = dict(zip(batch_axes, batch_shape, strict=True))
    # L z, one slab per sample, batch axes restored
    draws = rearrange(draws, pattern, **batch_sizes)
    dtype = jnp.result_type(mean, draws)
    # x = μ + L z
    return mean.astype(dtype) + draws.astype(dtype)

docs.text:
Joint draws of a partitioned Gaussian, and conditional draws from them.

[x_a; x_b] ~ 𝒩([μ_a; μ_b], [[Σ_aa, Σ_ab], [Σ_ba, Σ_bb]]),   Σ_ba = Σ_abᵀ

As in gaussx.conditional, B indexes the observed block and A the free one: with observed_index=1 (the default) A = a and B = b, and with observed_index=0 A = b and B = a. The joint draw uses the block factorisation

x_B = μ_B + L_B z₁,   L_B L_Bᵀ = Σ_BB
x_A = μ_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (x_B − μ_B) + Σ_A|B^½ z₂
Σ_A|B = Σ_AA − Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA

with x_B drawn by gaussx.sample_mvn, so the observed block keeps its structure, and Σ_A|B, the Schur complement of Σ_BB, the conditional covariance. The joint covariance, of size (N + M) × (N + M), is never formed.

When observed_value β is given, the conditional draws of x_A ∣ x_B = β reuse the same z₂:

x_A|β = x_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (β − x_B)
      = μ_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (β − μ_B) + Σ_A|B^½ z₂

which is exactly gaussx.matheron_update applied to the joint draws.

The Schur complement is dense in general: Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA is dense whatever the structure of Σ_AA, so Σ_A|B is factorised at O(N_A³) plus N_A solves against Σ_BB, with N_A = |A|. Its square root is the symmetric one from dense_symmetric_sqrt, with round-off negative eigenvalues clipped. That tolerates the rank deficiency of free points that coincide with observed ones (a Cholesky would return NaNs there), and its custom JVP keeps gradients finite when Σ_A|B has repeated eigenvalues.

Algorithm
  1. Draw the observed deviations x_B − μ_B = L_B z₁ with gaussx.sample_mvn.
  2. Form Σ_A|B and its symmetric square root Σ_A|B^½.
  3. Apply the gain G = Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ to the deviations, through the pseudo-inverse Σ_BB⁺ when Σ_BB is singular, and add Σ_A|B^½ z₂.
  4. When β is given, apply Matheron's update to the joint draws.

Block means (μ_a, μ_b).

required joint_covariance dict[str, AbstractLinearOperator]

Blocks {"aa": Σ_aa, "ab": Σ_ab, "bb": Σ_bb}; Σ_ba is Σ_ab.T.

PRNG key.

required observed_index int

Which block is observed: 1 for x_b (sample x_a ∣ x_b), 0 for x_a.

1 observed_value Float[Array, ' K'] | None

Optional value β of the observed block x_B. When given, the result also holds conditional draws.

None num_samples int

Number of independent draws.

1 solver AbstractSolveStrategy | None

Optional solver strategy for the solves against Σ_BB (e.g. gaussx.CGSolver). When None, routes through structural dispatch, as gaussx.matheron_update does.

None

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, Any]

{"joint": (samples_a, samples_b)} with shapes

dict[str, Any]

(num_samples, N) and (num_samples, M), plus

dict[str, Any]

"conditional", one draw of x_A ∣ x_B = β per row, when

dict[str, Any]

observed_value is given.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

On a missing covariance block, mismatched shapes, observed_index outside {0, 1} or num_samples below one.

Examples:

Condition two entries on a third:

>>> import jax
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> psd = lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
>>> cross = jnp.array([[1.0], [0.5]])
>>> blocks = {
...     "aa": lx.MatrixLinearOperator(2.0 * jnp.eye(2), psd),
...     "ab": lx.MatrixLinearOperator(cross),
...     "bb": lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(1), psd),
... }
>>> means = (jnp.zeros(2), jnp.zeros(1))
>>> result = gaussx.sample_joint_conditional(
...     means,
...     blocks,
...     key=jax.random.key(0),
...     observed_value=jnp.array([0.5]),
...     num_samples=3,
... )
>>> samples_a, samples_b = result["joint"]
>>> samples_a.shape, samples_b.shape, result["conditional"].shape

The conditional draws are Matheron's update of the joint ones (here Σ_bb = 1, so the gain is Σ_ab):

>>> expected = samples_a + (0.5 - samples_b) * cross[:, 0]
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(result["conditional"], expected, atol=1e-5))
True

>>> flipped = gaussx.sample_joint_conditional(
...     means, blocks, key=jax.random.key(1), observed_index=0
... )
>>> sorted(flipped)
['joint']

def sample_joint_conditional(
    joint_mean: tuple[Float[Array, " N"], Float[Array, " M"]],
    joint_covariance: dict[str, lx.AbstractLinearOperator],
    *,
    key: jax.Array,
    observed_index: int = 1,
    observed_value: Float[Array, " K"] | None = None,
    num_samples: int = 1,
    solver: AbstractSolveStrategy | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Joint draws of a partitioned Gaussian, and conditional draws from them.

        [x_a; x_b] ~ 𝒩([μ_a; μ_b], [[Σ_aa, Σ_ab], [Σ_ba, Σ_bb]]),   Σ_ba = Σ_abᵀ

    As in `gaussx.conditional`, B indexes the observed block and A the free
    one: with ``observed_index=1`` (the default) A = a and B = b, and with
    ``observed_index=0`` A = b and B = a. The joint draw uses the block
    factorisation

        x_B = μ_B + L_B z₁,   L_B L_Bᵀ = Σ_BB
        x_A = μ_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (x_B − μ_B) + Σ_A|B^½ z₂
        Σ_A|B = Σ_AA − Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA

    with x_B drawn by `gaussx.sample_mvn`, so the observed block keeps its
    structure, and Σ_A|B, the Schur complement of Σ_BB, the conditional
    covariance. The joint covariance, of size (N + M) × (N + M), is never
    formed.

    When ``observed_value`` β is given, the conditional draws of
    x_A ∣ x_B = β reuse the same z₂:

        x_A|β = x_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (β − x_B)
              = μ_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (β − μ_B) + Σ_A|B^½ z₂

    which is exactly `gaussx.matheron_update` applied to the joint draws.

    The Schur complement is dense in general: Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ Σ_BA is dense
    whatever the structure of Σ_AA, so Σ_A|B is factorised at O(N_A³)
    plus N_A solves against Σ_BB, with N_A = |A|. Its square root is the
    symmetric one from ``dense_symmetric_sqrt``, with round-off negative
    eigenvalues clipped. That tolerates the rank deficiency of free points
    that coincide with observed ones (a Cholesky would return NaNs there),
    and its custom JVP keeps gradients finite when Σ_A|B has repeated
    eigenvalues.

    Algorithm:
        1. Draw the observed deviations x_B − μ_B = L_B z₁ with
           `gaussx.sample_mvn`.
        2. Form Σ_A|B and its symmetric square root Σ_A|B^½.
        3. Apply the gain G = Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ to the deviations, through the
           pseudo-inverse Σ_BB⁺ when Σ_BB is singular, and add Σ_A|B^½ z₂.
        4. When β is given, apply Matheron's update to the joint draws.

    Args:
        joint_mean: Block means ``(μ_a, μ_b)``.
        joint_covariance: Blocks ``{"aa": Σ_aa, "ab": Σ_ab, "bb": Σ_bb}``;
            Σ_ba is ``Σ_ab.T``.
        key: PRNG key.
        observed_index: Which block is observed: ``1`` for x_b (sample
            x_a ∣ x_b), ``0`` for x_a.
        observed_value: Optional value β of the observed block x_B. When
            given, the result also holds conditional draws.
        num_samples: Number of independent draws.
        solver: Optional solver strategy for the solves against Σ_BB
            (e.g. `gaussx.CGSolver`). When ``None``, routes through
            structural dispatch, as `gaussx.matheron_update` does.

    Returns:
        ``{"joint": (samples_a, samples_b)}`` with shapes
        ``(num_samples, N)`` and ``(num_samples, M)``, plus
        ``"conditional"``, one draw of x_A ∣ x_B = β per row, when
        ``observed_value`` is given.

    Raises:
        ValueError: On a missing covariance block, mismatched shapes,
            ``observed_index`` outside ``{0, 1}`` or ``num_samples`` below
            one.

    Examples:
        Condition two entries on a third:

        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> psd = lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
        >>> cross = jnp.array([[1.0], [0.5]])
        >>> blocks = {
        ...     "aa": lx.MatrixLinearOperator(2.0 * jnp.eye(2), psd),
        ...     "ab": lx.MatrixLinearOperator(cross),
        ...     "bb": lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(1), psd),
        ... }
        >>> means = (jnp.zeros(2), jnp.zeros(1))
        >>> result = gaussx.sample_joint_conditional(
        ...     means,
        ...     blocks,
        ...     key=jax.random.key(0),
        ...     observed_value=jnp.array([0.5]),
        ...     num_samples=3,
        ... )
        >>> samples_a, samples_b = result["joint"]
        >>> samples_a.shape, samples_b.shape, result["conditional"].shape
        ((3, 2), (3, 1), (3, 2))

        The conditional draws are Matheron's update of the joint ones (here
        Σ_bb = 1, so the gain is Σ_ab):

        >>> expected = samples_a + (0.5 - samples_b) * cross[:, 0]
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(result["conditional"], expected, atol=1e-5))
        True

        Without an observed value there are only joint draws:

        >>> flipped = gaussx.sample_joint_conditional(
        ...     means, blocks, key=jax.random.key(1), observed_index=0
        ... )
        >>> sorted(flipped)
        ['joint']
    """
    mean_a, mean_b = (jnp.asarray(mean) for mean in joint_mean)
    covariance_aa, covariance_ab, covariance_bb = _covariance_blocks(
        joint_covariance, mean_a.shape, mean_b.shape
    )
    if observed_index not in (0, 1):
        raise ValueError(f"observed_index must be 0 or 1, got {observed_index}.")
    if num_samples < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"num_samples must be at least 1, got {num_samples}.")

    # --- index sets ---
    if observed_index == 1:
        # B = b, A = a
        observed_mean, free_mean = mean_b, mean_a
        observed_covariance, free_covariance = covariance_bb, covariance_aa
        # Σ_AB = Σ_ab
        cross_covariance = covariance_ab
    else:
        # B = a, A = b
        observed_mean, free_mean = mean_a, mean_b
        observed_covariance, free_covariance = covariance_aa, covariance_bb
        # Σ_AB = Σ_ba = Σ_abᵀ, a lazy operator transpose
        cross_covariance = covariance_ab.T

    if observed_value is not None:
        observed_value = jnp.asarray(observed_value)
        if observed_value.shape != observed_mean.shape:
            raise ValueError(
                f"observed_value must have shape {observed_mean.shape}, got "
                f"{observed_value.shape}."
            )

    if solver is None:
        solve_observed = lambda vector: solve(observed_covariance, vector)
    else:
        solve_observed = lambda vector: dispatch_solve(
            observed_covariance, vector, solver
        )

    def gain(deviations: Float[Array, "S K"]) -> Float[Array, "S T"]:
        """Apply the gain G = Σ_AB Σ_BB⁺ to each row.

        The structured solve is used whenever it succeeds. A singular (only
        semi-definite) Σ_BB makes it return non-finite values, and then the
        batch is redone with the pseudo-inverse Σ_BB⁺: for a valid joint
        covariance both the deviations and the rows of Σ_AB lie in the
        range of Σ_BB, where the pseudo-inverse is exact. ``lax.cond``
        evaluates only the branch it takes.

        Args:
            deviations: Rows d to map, each in the observed space.

        Returns:
            The rows G d, each in the free space.
        """
        # Σ_BB⁻¹ d, one row at a time
        solved = jax.vmap(solve_observed)(deviations)
        all_finite = jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(solved))
        # Σ_BB⁺ d when the structured solve failed
        solved = jax.lax.cond(
            all_finite,
            lambda: solved,
            lambda: _pseudo_inverse_solve(observed_covariance, deviations),
        )
        # G d = Σ_AB Σ_BB⁺ d
        return jax.vmap(cross_covariance.mv)(solved)

    # --- joint draws ---
    observed_key, schur_key = jr.split(key)
    # x_B − μ_B = L_B z₁
    observed_deviations = sample_mvn(
        jnp.zeros_like(observed_mean),
        observed_covariance,
        key=observed_key,
        num_samples=num_samples,
    )
    dtype = observed_deviations.dtype
    # Σ_A|B^½
    schur_root = _schur_root(free_covariance, cross_covariance, gain)
    # z₂ ~ 𝒩(0, I), one row per draw
    noise = jr.normal(schur_key, (num_samples, free_mean.shape[0]), dtype=dtype)
    # Σ_A|B^½ z₂
    conditional_deviations = einsum(noise, schur_root, "draw col, row col -> draw row")

    # x_B = μ_B + L_B z₁
    observed_samples = observed_mean + observed_deviations
    # Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (x_B − μ_B)
    gained_deviations = gain(observed_deviations)
    # x_A = μ_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (x_B − μ_B) + Σ_A|B^½ z₂
    free_samples = free_mean + gained_deviations + conditional_deviations
    if observed_index == 1:
        joint = (free_samples, observed_samples)
    else:
        joint = (observed_samples, free_samples)
    result: dict[str, Any] = {"joint": joint}

    # --- conditional draws ---
    if observed_value is not None:
        # Matheron's update of the returned joint draws, literally: with a
        # finite-tolerance solver the gain is not additive across right-hand
        # sides, so shifting from the mean instead would drift from it.
        # β − x_B
        observed_residual = observed_value - observed_samples
        # x_A|β = x_A + Σ_AB Σ_BB⁻¹ (β − x_B)
        result["conditional"] = free_samples + gain(observed_residual)
    return result

The Gaussian in natural form: the natural parameters \((\boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{\mu}, -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{\Lambda})\), held in the fields eta1 and eta2. Conversions between mean/covariance, natural, and expectation parameterizations — multivariate (operator-aware) and univariate (per-site diagonal) — plus the log-partition, Fisher information, and sufficient statistics that natural-gradient and EP updates are built from.

Structured linear algebra and Gaussian primitives for JAX.

Bases: Module

Gaussian 𝒩(μ, Σ) held by its natural parameters (Λ μ, −½ Λ).

log 𝒩(x; μ, Σ) = xᵀ Λ μ + tr(−½ Λ x xᵀ) − log_partition(Λ μ, −½ Λ)
log_partition(Λ μ, −½ Λ) = ½ μᵀ Λ μ − ½ log det Λ + ½ D_x log 2π

with the precision Λ = Σ⁻¹ and the sufficient statistics (x, x xᵀ). The base measure is one, so the normaliser (2π)^(−D_x/2) lives in the log-partition, which log_partition returns.

Attributes:

Name Type Description eta1 Float[Array, ' N']

Precision-weighted mean Λ μ, the first natural parameter.

eta2 AbstractLinearOperator

Scaled precision −½ Λ, the second natural parameter, as an operator.

Examples:

From a mean and a covariance Σ = 2 I:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> mean = jnp.array([1.0, -1.0])
>>> covariance = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
...     2.0 * jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
... )
>>> expfam = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(mean, covariance)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(expfam.eta1, jnp.array([0.5, -0.5])))
True
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(expfam.eta2.as_matrix(), -0.25 * jnp.eye(2)))
True

From the precision Λ = Σ⁻¹ the natural parameters agree:

>>> precision = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
...     0.5 * jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
... )
>>> same = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_prec(mean, precision)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(same.eta1, expfam.eta1))
True

class GaussianExpFam(eqx.Module):
    """Gaussian 𝒩(μ, Σ) held by its natural parameters (Λ μ, −½ Λ).

        log 𝒩(x; μ, Σ) = xᵀ Λ μ + tr(−½ Λ x xᵀ) − log_partition(Λ μ, −½ Λ)
        log_partition(Λ μ, −½ Λ) = ½ μᵀ Λ μ − ½ log det Λ + ½ D_x log 2π

    with the precision Λ = Σ⁻¹ and the sufficient statistics (x, x xᵀ). The
    base measure is one, so the normaliser (2π)^(−D_x/2) lives in the
    log-partition, which `log_partition` returns.

    Attributes:
        eta1: Precision-weighted mean Λ μ, the first natural parameter.
        eta2: Scaled precision −½ Λ, the second natural parameter, as an
            operator.

    Examples:
        From a mean and a covariance Σ = 2 I:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> mean = jnp.array([1.0, -1.0])
        >>> covariance = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
        ...     2.0 * jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
        ... )
        >>> expfam = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(mean, covariance)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(expfam.eta1, jnp.array([0.5, -0.5])))
        True
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(expfam.eta2.as_matrix(), -0.25 * jnp.eye(2)))
        True

        From the precision Λ = Σ⁻¹ the natural parameters agree:

        >>> precision = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
        ...     0.5 * jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
        ... )
        >>> same = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_prec(mean, precision)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(same.eta1, expfam.eta1))
        True
    """

    eta1: Float[Array, " N"]
    eta2: lx.AbstractLinearOperator

    @staticmethod
    def from_mean_cov(
        mu: Float[Array, " N"],
        Sigma: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> GaussianExpFam:
        """Natural-form Gaussian from its mean μ and covariance Σ.

            Λ μ = Σ⁻¹ μ,   −½ Λ = −½ Σ⁻¹

        Args:
            mu: Mean μ.
            Sigma: Covariance Σ.

        Returns:
            The `GaussianExpFam` with natural parameters (Λ μ, −½ Λ).

        Examples:
            >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
            >>> import lineax as lx
            >>> import gaussx
            >>> covariance = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.array([2.0, 4.0]))
            >>> expfam = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(jnp.ones(2), covariance)
            >>> bool(jnp.allclose(expfam.eta1, jnp.array([0.5, 0.25])))
            True
        """
        eta1, eta2 = mean_cov_to_natural(mu, Sigma)
        return GaussianExpFam(eta1=eta1, eta2=eta2)

    @staticmethod
    def from_mean_prec(
        mu: Float[Array, " N"],
        Lambda: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> GaussianExpFam:
        """Natural-form Gaussian from its mean μ and precision Λ, with no solve.

            (Λ μ, −½ Λ)

        Args:
            mu: Mean μ.
            Lambda: Precision Λ = Σ⁻¹.

        Returns:
            The `GaussianExpFam` with natural parameters (Λ μ, −½ Λ).

        Examples:
            >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
            >>> import lineax as lx
            >>> import gaussx
            >>> precision = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.array([2.0, 4.0]))
            >>> expfam = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_prec(jnp.ones(2), precision)

def mean_cov_to_natural(
    mu: Float[Array, " N"],
    Sigma: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    *,
    solver: AbstractSolverStrategy | None = None,
) -> tuple[Float[Array, " N"], lx.AbstractLinearOperator]:
    """Natural parameters (Λ μ, −½ Λ) from the mean and covariance, in operator form.

        Λ μ = Σ⁻¹ μ,   −½ Λ = −½ Σ⁻¹

    The solve and the lazy inverse dispatch on the structure of Σ
    (diagonal, Kronecker, …). For dense arrays see `mean_chol_to_natural`;
    for a block-tridiagonal chain, `gaussx.ssm_to_naturals`.

    Args:
        mu: Mean μ.
        Sigma: Covariance Σ.
        solver: Solver strategy for Σ; ``None`` uses structural dispatch.

    Returns:
        Tuple ``(eta1, eta2)`` holding Λ μ and −½ Λ as a lazy operator.

    Examples:
        A diagonal covariance Σ = diag(2, 4):

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> covariance = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.array([2.0, 4.0]))
        >>> eta1, eta2 = gaussx.mean_cov_to_natural(jnp.ones(2), covariance)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(eta1, jnp.array([0.5, 0.25])))
        True
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(eta2.as_matrix(), jnp.diag(jnp.array([-0.25, -0.125]))))
        True
    """
    # Λ μ = Σ⁻¹ μ
    eta1 = dispatch_solve(Sigma, mu, solver)
    # Λ = Σ⁻¹, lazy
    precision = inv(Sigma)
    # −½ Λ
    eta2 = -0.5 * precision
    return eta1, eta2

Λ μ = L⁻ᵀ L⁻¹ μ,   −½ Λ = −½ L⁻ᵀ L⁻¹,   L Lᵀ = Σ

Both come from triangular solves against L. No solver is exposed: the systems are triangular, not symmetric positive definite, so the iterative strategies (CG, BBMM, preconditioned CG, MINRES) do not apply.

  2. Solve L Lᵀ Λ = I the same way and scale by −½.
  3. With batch axes, flatten them, vmap steps 1 and 2, and restore them.

Leading batch axes are kept:

>>> eta1, eta2 = gaussx.mean_chol_to_natural(jnp.ones((4, 2, 3)), factors)
>>> eta1.shape, eta2.shape

def mean_chol_to_natural(
    mu: Float[Array, "*batch N"],
    S_sqrt: Float[Array, "*batch N N"],
) -> tuple[Float[Array, "*batch N"], Float[Array, "*batch N N"]]:
    """Natural parameters (Λ μ, −½ Λ) from the mean and the Cholesky factor of Σ.

        Λ μ = L⁻ᵀ L⁻¹ μ,   −½ Λ = −½ L⁻ᵀ L⁻¹,   L Lᵀ = Σ

    Both come from triangular solves against L. No solver is exposed: the
    systems are triangular, not symmetric positive definite, so the
    iterative strategies (CG, BBMM, preconditioned CG, MINRES) do not apply.

    Algorithm:
        1. Solve L Lᵀ (Λ μ) = μ by two triangular solves.
        2. Solve L Lᵀ Λ = I the same way and scale by −½.
        3. With batch axes, flatten them, vmap steps 1 and 2, and restore them.

    Args:
        mu: Mean μ, with any number of leading batch axes.
        S_sqrt: Lower Cholesky factor L of the covariance, L Lᵀ = Σ.

    Returns:
        Tuple ``(eta1, eta2)`` holding Λ μ and −½ Λ.

    Examples:
        A diagonal factor L = diag(1, 2), so Σ = diag(1, 4):

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> factor = jnp.diag(jnp.array([1.0, 2.0]))
        >>> eta1, eta2 = gaussx.mean_chol_to_natural(jnp.ones(2), factor)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(eta1, jnp.array([1.0, 0.25])))
        True
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(eta2, jnp.diag(jnp.array([-0.5, -0.125]))))
        True

        Leading batch axes are kept:

        >>> factors = jnp.broadcast_to(jnp.eye(3), (4, 2, 3, 3))
        >>> eta1, eta2 = gaussx.mean_chol_to_natural(jnp.ones((4, 2, 3)), factors)
        >>> eta1.shape, eta2.shape
        ((4, 2, 3), (4, 2, 3, 3))
    """

    def _core(mean: Float[Array, " N"], factor: Float[Array, "N N"]):
        # Λ μ = Σ⁻¹ μ = L⁻ᵀ L⁻¹ μ
        precision_mean = jax.scipy.linalg.cho_solve((factor, True), mean)
        event_size = factor.shape[0]
        identity = jnp.eye(event_size, dtype=factor.dtype)
        # Λ = Σ⁻¹ = L⁻ᵀ L⁻¹ I, one matrix solve
        precision = jax.scipy.linalg.cho_solve((factor, True), identity)
        # −½ Λ
        scaled_precision = -0.5 * precision
        return precision_mean, scaled_precision

    *batch, event_size = mu.shape
    if not batch:
        return _core(mu, S_sqrt)
    # reshape, not einx: einx rejects the zero-length axis of an empty batch
    mean_flat = mu.reshape(-1, event_size)
    factor_flat = S_sqrt.reshape(-1, event_size, event_size)
    eta1_flat, eta2_flat = jax.vmap(_core)(mean_flat, factor_flat)
    return eta1_flat.reshape(mu.shape), eta2_flat.reshape(S_sqrt.shape)

    eta2: Float[Array, "*batch N N"],
    *,
    solver: AbstractSolverStrategy | None = None,

    """Mean μ and Cholesky factor of Σ from the natural parameters (Λ μ, −½ Λ).

        Λ = −2 (−½ Λ),   μ = Λ⁻¹ (Λ μ),   Σ = Λ⁻¹,   L Lᵀ = Σ

    Algorithm:
        1. Form Λ = −2 (−½ Λ) as a PSD-tagged operator.
        2. Solve Λ μ for μ.
        3. Invert Λ to the dense Σ and factor Σ = L Lᵀ.
        4. With batch axes, flatten them, vmap steps 1 to 3, and restore them.

    Args:
        eta1: Precision-weighted mean Λ μ, with any number of leading batch
            axes.
        eta2: Scaled precision −½ Λ.
        solver: Solver strategy for Λ; ``None`` uses structural dispatch.

    Returns:

        factor L of the covariance.

    Examples:
        A diagonal precision Λ = diag(1, 4):

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> eta2 = jnp.diag(jnp.array([-0.5, -2.0]))
        >>> mean, factor = gaussx.natural_to_mean_chol(jnp.array([1.0, 4.0]), eta2)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(mean, 1.0))
        True
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(factor, jnp.diag(jnp.array([1.0, 0.5]))))
        True

        >>> factor = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.5, 2.0]])
        >>> naturals = gaussx.mean_chol_to_natural(jnp.array([1.0, -1.0]), factor)
        >>> _, factor_back = gaussx.natural_to_mean_chol(*naturals)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(factor_back, factor, atol=1e-5))

        precision_mean: Float[Array, " N"], scaled_precision: Float[Array, "N N"]

        precision_matrix = -2.0 * scaled_precision
        precision = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
            precision_matrix, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag

        # Σ = Λ⁻¹
        covariance_matrix = inv(precision).as_matrix()
        covariance = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(

        moment 𝔼[x xᵀ].

    m2: Float[Array, "*batch N N"],

        2. Solve Σ for Λ μ, then against the identity for Λ = Σ⁻¹.
        3. Scale Λ by −½.
        4. With batch axes, flatten them, vmap steps 1 to 3, and restore them.

    Args:
        m1: First moment 𝔼[x] = μ, with any number of leading batch axes.
        m2: Second moment 𝔼[x xᵀ] = Σ + μ μᵀ.
        solver: Solver strategy for Σ; ``None`` uses structural dispatch.

        >>> import gaussx
        >>> second = 2.0 * jnp.eye(2) + jnp.ones((2, 2))
        >>> eta1, eta2 = gaussx.expectation_to_natural(jnp.ones(2), second)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(eta1, 0.5)), bool(jnp.allclose(eta2, -0.25 * jnp.eye(2)))

        Leading batch axes are kept:

        >>> seconds = jnp.broadcast_to(jnp.eye(3), (4, 3, 3))
        >>> eta1, eta2 = gaussx.expectation_to_natural(jnp.zeros((4, 3)), seconds)
        >>> eta1.shape, eta2.shape
        ((4, 3), (4, 3, 3))

        # Σ = 𝔼[x xᵀ] − μ μᵀ
        covariance_matrix = second_moment - mean_outer
        covariance = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
            covariance_matrix, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag

        precision_mean = dispatch_solve(covariance, first_moment, solver)

    return eta1_flat.reshape(m1.shape), eta2_flat.reshape(m2.shape)

Log-partition of a Gaussian in natural form, normaliser included.

log_partition(Λ μ, −½ Λ) = −¼ (Λ μ)ᵀ (−½ Λ)⁻¹ (Λ μ) − ½ log det Λ
                           + ½ D_x log 2π
                         = ½ μᵀ Λ μ − ½ log det Λ + ½ D_x log 2π

The base measure is one (see GaussianExpFam), so xᵀ Λ μ + tr(−½ Λ x xᵀ) − log_partition(Λ μ, −½ Λ) is the normalised log-density log 𝒩(x; μ, Σ).

Name Type Description Default expfam GaussianExpFam

Gaussian in natural form (Λ μ, −½ Λ).

required

Examples:

A standard normal in two dimensions has log-partition log 2π:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> identity = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
>>> standard = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(jnp.zeros(2), identity)
>>> round(float(gaussx.log_partition(standard)), 4)

A mean μ adds ½ μᵀ Λ μ:

>>> mean = jnp.array([2.0, 0.0])
>>> shifted = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(mean, identity)
>>> difference = gaussx.log_partition(shifted) - gaussx.log_partition(standard)
>>> round(float(difference), 4)
2.0

def log_partition(expfam: GaussianExpFam) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Log-partition of a Gaussian in natural form, normaliser included.

        log_partition(Λ μ, −½ Λ) = −¼ (Λ μ)ᵀ (−½ Λ)⁻¹ (Λ μ) − ½ log det Λ
                                   + ½ D_x log 2π
                                 = ½ μᵀ Λ μ − ½ log det Λ + ½ D_x log 2π

    The base measure is one (see `GaussianExpFam`), so
    xᵀ Λ μ + tr(−½ Λ x xᵀ) − log_partition(Λ μ, −½ Λ) is the normalised
    log-density log 𝒩(x; μ, Σ).

    Args:
        expfam: Gaussian in natural form (Λ μ, −½ Λ).

    Returns:
        The scalar log-partition.

    Examples:
        A standard normal in two dimensions has log-partition log 2π:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> identity = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
        >>> standard = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(jnp.zeros(2), identity)
        >>> round(float(gaussx.log_partition(standard)), 4)
        1.8379

        A mean μ adds ½ μᵀ Λ μ:

        >>> mean = jnp.array([2.0, 0.0])
        >>> shifted = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(mean, identity)
        >>> difference = gaussx.log_partition(shifted) - gaussx.log_partition(standard)
        >>> round(float(difference), 4)
        2.0
    """
    # Λ = −2 (−½ Λ)
    precision = -2.0 * expfam.eta2
    event_size = precision.in_size()

    # (−½ Λ)⁻¹ Λ μ = −2 μ
    minus_two_mean = solve(expfam.eta2, expfam.eta1)
    # −¼ (Λ μ)ᵀ (−½ Λ)⁻¹ (Λ μ) = ½ μᵀ Λ μ
    quadratic_term = -0.25 * (expfam.eta1 @ minus_two_mean)

    # −½ log det Λ
    logdet_term = -0.5 * logdet(precision)

    # log_partition = ½ μᵀ Λ μ − ½ log det Λ + ½ D_x log 2π
    return quadratic_term + logdet_term + 0.5 * event_size * _LOG_2PI

) -> lx.AbstractLinearOperator:
    """Fisher information of the mean μ, which is the precision Λ = Σ⁻¹.

        𝔼[∇_μ log 𝒩(x; μ, Σ) ∇_μ log 𝒩(x; μ, Σ)ᵀ] = Λ = −2 (−½ Λ)

    This is the μ block that natural-gradient descent on a
    (μ, Σ)-parameterised objective uses. It is **not** the Fisher
    information in natural coordinates, the Hessian of the log-partition
    with respect to (Λ μ, −½ Λ): that is the (D_x + D_x²)-dimensional
    covariance of the sufficient statistics (x, x xᵀ), whose Λ μ block is
    Σ, not Λ.

    Args:
        expfam: Gaussian in natural form (Λ μ, −½ Λ).

    Returns:
        The precision Λ as an operator.

    Examples:
        A covariance of 2 I has Fisher information ½ I:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> covariance = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
        ...     2.0 * jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
        ... )
        >>> expfam = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(jnp.ones(2), covariance)
        >>> information = gaussx.fisher_info(expfam)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(information.as_matrix(), 0.5 * jnp.eye(2)))
        True
    """
    # Λ = −2 (−½ Λ)
    return -2.0 * expfam.eta2

def sufficient_stats(
    x: Float[Array, "*batch N"],
) -> tuple[Float[Array, "*batch N"], Float[Array, "*batch N N"]]:
    """Sufficient statistics (x, x xᵀ) of a Gaussian, over any batch axes.

        (x, x xᵀ)

    Args:
        x: Points x, with any number of leading batch axes.

    Returns:
        Tuple ``(x, outer_product)`` holding x itself and x xᵀ, one D_x × D_x
        matrix per point.

    Examples:
        Four points in three dimensions:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> points = jnp.ones((4, 3))
        >>> first, second = gaussx.sufficient_stats(points)
        >>> first.shape, second.shape
        ((4, 3), (4, 3, 3))

        A single point gives its outer product:

        >>> _, outer = gaussx.sufficient_stats(jnp.array([1.0, 2.0]))
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(outer, jnp.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 4.0]])))
        True
    """
    # x xᵀ
    outer_product = einsum(x, x, "... row, ... col -> ... row col")

docs.title: kl_divergence(q: GaussianExpFam, p: GaussianExpFam) -> Float[Array, '']
docs.text:
KL(first ‖ second): KL[q ‖ p] in the Bregman form on natural parameters.

KL[q ‖ p] = log_partition(p) − log_partition(q)
            − (Λ_p μ_p − Λ_q μ_q)ᵀ 𝔼_q[x]
            − tr((−½ Λ_p + ½ Λ_q) 𝔼_q[x xᵀ])

with log_partition(p) and log_partition(q) taken at the natural parameters of p and q, and q's expectation parameters (𝔼_q[x], 𝔼_q[x xᵀ]) = (μ_q, Σ_q + μ_q μ_qᵀ), the gradient of the log-partition at q. The first argument is the distribution the expectation is taken under, whatever its parameter name: kl_divergence(a, b) is KL[a ‖ b]. Mathematically equal to gaussian_kl with its arguments in the same order; this form keeps the gradient in natural-parameter space, for use inside a natural-gradient loop.

Algorithm
  1. Evaluate the log-partitions of p and q.
  2. Recover μ_q and Σ_q from q's natural parameters (to_mean_cov).
  3. Contract Λ_p μ_p − Λ_q μ_q with 𝔼_q[x] = μ_q.
  4. Split the second-moment term into a quadratic form in μ_q, by operator matvecs, and two gaussx.trace_product calls against Σ_q, so neither −½ Λ nor Σ_q is materialised.
  5. Combine the terms.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default q GaussianExpFam

First Gaussian q, the one the expectation is taken under.

required p GaussianExpFam

Second Gaussian p.

required

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, '']

The scalar KL divergence KL[q ‖ p].

Examples:

It agrees with gaussian_kl in mean and covariance form:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import gaussx
>>> q_cov = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
>>> p_cov = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
...     2.0 * jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
... )
>>> q_mean, p_mean = jnp.zeros(2), jnp.array([1.0, 0.0])
>>> q = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(q_mean, q_cov)
>>> p = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(p_mean, p_cov)
>>> kl = gaussx.kl_divergence(q, p)
>>> round(float(kl), 4)
0.4431
>>> reference = gaussx.gaussian_kl(q_mean, q_cov, p_mean, p_cov)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(kl, reference, atol=1e-5))
True

The divergence of a Gaussian from itself is zero:

>>> bool(jnp.allclose(gaussx.kl_divergence(q, q), 0.0, atol=1e-5))
True
Source code in src/gaussx/_expfam/_gaussian.py 
def kl_divergence(
    q: GaussianExpFam,
    p: GaussianExpFam,
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """KL(first ‖ second): KL[q ‖ p] in the Bregman form on natural parameters.

        KL[q ‖ p] = log_partition(p) − log_partition(q)
                    − (Λ_p μ_p − Λ_q μ_q)ᵀ 𝔼_q[x]
                    − tr((−½ Λ_p + ½ Λ_q) 𝔼_q[x xᵀ])

    with log_partition(p) and log_partition(q) taken at the natural
    parameters of p and q, and q's expectation parameters
    (𝔼_q[x], 𝔼_q[x xᵀ]) = (μ_q, Σ_q + μ_q μ_qᵀ), the gradient of the
    log-partition at q. The first argument is the distribution the
    expectation is taken under, whatever its parameter name:
    ``kl_divergence(a, b)`` is KL[a ‖ b]. Mathematically equal to
    `gaussian_kl` with its arguments in the same order; this form keeps the
    gradient in natural-parameter space, for use inside a natural-gradient
    loop.

    Algorithm:
        1. Evaluate the log-partitions of p and q.
        2. Recover μ_q and Σ_q from q's natural parameters (`to_mean_cov`).
        3. Contract Λ_p μ_p − Λ_q μ_q with 𝔼_q[x] = μ_q.
        4. Split the second-moment term into a quadratic form in μ_q, by
           operator matvecs, and two `gaussx.trace_product` calls against
           Σ_q, so neither −½ Λ nor Σ_q is materialised.
        5. Combine the terms.

    Args:
        q: First Gaussian q, the one the expectation is taken under.
        p: Second Gaussian p.

    Returns:
        The scalar KL divergence KL[q ‖ p].

    Examples:
        It agrees with `gaussian_kl` in mean and covariance form:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import gaussx
        >>> q_cov = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
        >>> p_cov = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
        ...     2.0 * jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
        ... )
        >>> q_mean, p_mean = jnp.zeros(2), jnp.array([1.0, 0.0])
        >>> q = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(q_mean, q_cov)
        >>> p = gaussx.GaussianExpFam.from_mean_cov(p_mean, p_cov)
        >>> kl = gaussx.kl_divergence(q, p)
        >>> round(float(kl), 4)
        0.4431
        >>> reference = gaussx.gaussian_kl(q_mean, q_cov, p_mean, p_cov)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(kl, reference, atol=1e-5))
        True

        The divergence of a Gaussian from itself is zero:

        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(gaussx.kl_divergence(q, q), 0.0, atol=1e-5))
        True
    """
    # --- log-partitions ---
    # log_partition(p) = ½ μ_pᵀ Λ_p μ_p − ½ log det Λ_p + ½ D_x log 2π
    p_log_partition = log_partition(p)
    # log_partition(q) = ½ μ_qᵀ Λ_q μ_q − ½ log det Λ_q + ½ D_x log 2π
    q_log_partition = log_partition(q)

    # --- expectation parameters of q ---
    # (μ_q, Σ_q), so that 𝔼_q[x] = μ_q and 𝔼_q[x xᵀ] = Σ_q + μ_q μ_qᵀ
    q_mean, q_covariance = to_mean_cov(q)

    # --- first natural parameter ---
    # Λ_p μ_p − Λ_q μ_q
    precision_mean_difference = p.eta1 - q.eta1
    # (Λ_p μ_p − Λ_q μ_q)ᵀ μ_q
    linear_term = precision_mean_difference @ q_mean

    # --- second natural parameter ---
    # tr((−½ Λ_p + ½ Λ_q)(Σ_q + μ_q μ_qᵀ))
    #   = μ_qᵀ (−½ Λ_p + ½ Λ_q) μ_q + tr(−½ Λ_p Σ_q) − tr(−½ Λ_q Σ_q)
    # −½ Λ_p μ_q
    p_scaled_mean = p.eta2.mv(q_mean)
    # −½ Λ_q μ_q
    q_scaled_mean = q.eta2.mv(q_mean)
    # (−½ Λ_p + ½ Λ_q) μ_q
    scaled_mean_difference = p_scaled_mean - q_scaled_mean
    # μ_qᵀ (−½ Λ_p + ½ Λ_q) μ_q
    quadratic_term = q_mean @ scaled_mean_difference
    # tr(−½ Λ_p Σ_q)
    p_trace = trace_product(p.eta2, q_covariance)
    # tr(−½ Λ_q Σ_q)
    q_trace = trace_product(q.eta2, q_covariance)
    # tr((−½ Λ_p + ½ Λ_q) 𝔼_q[x xᵀ])
    second_moment_term = quadratic_term + p_trace - q_trace

    # KL[q ‖ p] = log_partition(p) − log_partition(q) − linear − second moment
    return p_log_partition - q_log_partition - linear_term - second_moment_term
