docs.title: Solver Strategies¶
docs.text:
gaussx decouples what you compute (solve, logdet) from how it is computed (dense factorization, iterative CG, LSMR, etc.) via solver strategies.

What you'll learn:

  1. How solver strategies decouple algorithms from models
  2. Comparing all 7 full strategies: DenseSolver, CGSolver, AutoSolver, BBMMSolver, PreconditionedCGSolver, LSMRSolver, ComposedSolver
  3. Standalone logdet strategies: SLQLogdet, DenseLogdet, IndefiniteSLQLogdet
  4. Fine-grained composition via ComposedSolver
  5. When to use which strategy

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
gaussx separates solve and logdet into independent protocol axes:

  • AbstractSolveStrategy -- just .solve(op, b)
  • AbstractLogdetStrategy -- just .logdet(op)
  • AbstractSolverStrategy -- bundles both (inherits from both)

Convenience classes like CGSolver implement both methods, but you can also use standalone logdet strategies (SLQLogdet, DenseLogdet, IndefiniteSLQLogdet) and compose them freely via ComposedSolver.

For example, a MultivariateNormal distribution accepts a strategy object and delegates all linear algebra to it. During prototyping you might use DenseSolver; at scale you switch to CGSolver or BBMMSolver with a single-line change.

Conjugate Gradients (CG): For a PSD system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, CG minimizes $\Vert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^\star \Vert_{\mathbf{A}}$ over Krylov subspaces $\mathcal{K}_j(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{b})$, where $j$ counts CG iterations. After $j$ iterations, the error satisfies

$$\Vert \mathbf{x}^{(j)} - \mathbf{x}^\star \Vert_{\mathbf{A}} \le 2 \left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa} - 1}{\sqrt{\kappa} + 1}\right)^j \Vert \mathbf{x}^{(0)} - \mathbf{x}^\star \Vert_{\mathbf{A}}$$

where $\kappa = \gamma_{\max} / \gamma_{\min}$ is the condition number (Hestenes & Stiefel, 1952).

Stochastic Lanczos Quadrature (SLQ): Approximates $\log \det \mathbf{A} = \mathrm{tr}(\log \mathbf{A})$ using Hutchinson's trace estimator:

$$\log \det \mathbf{A} \approx \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^S \mathbf{z}_s^\top \log(\mathbf{A}) \mathbf{z}_s$$

where each $\mathbf{z}_s^\top \log(\mathbf{A}) \mathbf{z}_s$ is evaluated via the Lanczos decomposition (Ubaru et al., 2017).

docs.title: DenseSolver¶
docs.text: DenseSolver delegates to gaussx structural dispatch (gaussx.solve, gaussx.logdet). It automatically picks the best dense algorithm based on operator tags: Cholesky for PSD, block-diagonal factorization for BlockDiag, Kronecker eigendecomposition for Kronecker, etc.

docs.title: CGSolver¶
docs.text: CGSolver uses lineax CG for the solve and matfree stochastic Lanczos quadrature (SLQ) for the log-determinant. It works for any PSD operator, even matrix-free ones where as_matrix() is unavailable.

docs.title: AutoSolver¶
docs.text: AutoSolver inspects the operator type and size to automatically select the right backend. For structured operators (Diagonal, BlockDiag, Kronecker, LowRankUpdate) and small dense matrices it picks DenseSolver. For large PSD operators it switches to CGSolver.

docs.title: BBMMSolver¶
docs.text:
BBMMSolver carries the settings of the Black-Box Matrix-Matrix method (Gardner et al. 2018). Its solve is a CG solve and its logdet a stochastic Lanczos quadrature (SLQ) estimate, like CGSolver. solve_and_logdet is a convenience that calls the two in turn; it shares no matvecs.

The BBMM method (Gardner et al., 2018) was introduced in GPyTorch. It runs the right-hand sides and the SLQ probe vectors through one modified batched CG (mBCG) pass and reads the Lanczos tridiagonals for the logdet off the CG coefficients. In gaussx that shared pass is gaussx.inv_quad_logdet(op, rhs, strategy=BBMMSolver(...)). It is not automatically cheaper: it runs the probe columns to CG convergence rather than stopping after lanczos_order Lanczos steps, so on a well-conditioned kernel it can apply the operator to more columns than a separate solve and SLQ.

docs.title: PreconditionedCGSolver¶
docs.text:
PreconditionedCGSolver builds a low-rank partial Cholesky preconditioner via matfree, then runs preconditioned CG. For operators of the form $\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}$ (common in GP regression), preconditioning dramatically reduces the number of CG iterations required for convergence.

Preconditioning transforms the system to $\mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathbf{b}$ where $\mathbf{M} \approx \mathbf{A}$ is cheap to invert. For GP kernels of the form $\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}$, a rank-$r$ partial Cholesky approximation $\mathbf{R} \mathbf{R}^\top \approx \mathbf{K}$ gives $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{R}^\top + \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}$, which can be inverted via the Woodbury identity in $O(Nr^2)$. This dramatically improves the effective condition number.

The shift parameter should be set to the noise variance $\sigma^2$.

docs.title: LSMRSolver¶
docs.text:
LSMRSolver implements the LSMR algorithm (Fong & Saunders 2011). Unlike CG, LSMR works for rectangular and ill-conditioned systems too. It only requires matvec and transpose-matvec, and supports Tikhonov regularization via the damp parameter (minimizes $\Vert \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \Vert_2^2 + \beta \Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert_2^2$ with $\beta = \mathrm{damp}^2$).

LSMR (Fong & Saunders, 2011) is mathematically equivalent to MINRES applied to the normal equations $\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{b}$, but is numerically more stable. It is the natural choice when $\mathbf{A}$ is rectangular or when Tikhonov regularization ($\min \Vert \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \Vert_2^2 + \beta \Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert_2^2$) is desired.

docs.title: ComposedSolver¶
docs.text:
ComposedSolver lets you mix-and-match solve and logdet from different strategies. It accepts fine-grained protocols: any AbstractSolveStrategy for the solve side and any AbstractLogdetStrategy for the logdet side.

This means you can pair a full solver (like DenseSolver) with a standalone logdet strategy (like SLQLogdet) -- no need to wrap the logdet in a full solver class.

docs.title: Standalone Logdet Strategies¶
docs.text:
gaussx provides three standalone logdet strategies that implement AbstractLogdetStrategy:

  • SLQLogdet -- stochastic Lanczos quadrature for PSD operators
  • IndefiniteSLQLogdet -- SLQ with $\log \vert \gamma \vert$ for symmetric indefinite operators, with optional diagonal shift
  • DenseLogdet -- delegates to gaussx.logdet (structural dispatch)

These are the building blocks that CGSolver, BBMMSolver, etc. use internally for their logdet computation. By extracting them as standalone strategies, you can compose them freely.

docs.title: Standalone logdet strategies¶
docs.text:
Strategy Best for SLQLogdet Large PSD operators IndefiniteSLQLogdet Symmetric indefinite / shifted DenseLogdet Small-medium, structured

Details:

  • DenseSolver: Exploits Kronecker, BlockDiag, Diagonal fast paths via structural dispatch.
  • CGSolver: Works without as_matrix(); stochastic Lanczos quadrature (SLQ) for logdet.
  • AutoSolver: Inspects operator type and size, delegates to DenseSolver or CGSolver automatically.
  • BBMMSolver: GPyTorch-style settings; inv_quad_logdet runs its shared mBCG pass, while solve_and_logdet is a separate solve and SLQ.
  • PreconditionedCGSolver: Low-rank Cholesky preconditioner accelerates convergence on $\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}$.
  • LSMRSolver: Supports Tikhonov damping; only needs matvec and transpose-matvec.
  • ComposedSolver: Delegates solve and logdet to two independent strategies; pair exact solve with stochastic logdet, etc.
  • SLQLogdet / IndefiniteSLQLogdet / DenseLogdet: Standalone logdet strategies usable with ComposedSolver for fine-grained control.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• Solver strategies decouple algorithm choice from model code. Swap a single strategy object to change how solve and logdet are computed.
  • Fine-grained protocols (AbstractSolveStrategy, AbstractLogdetStrategy) let you compose solve and logdet independently via ComposedSolver.
  • Standalone logdet strategies (SLQLogdet, IndefiniteSLQLogdet, DenseLogdet) can be used directly with ComposedSolver for maximum flexibility -- no need to wrap logdet in a full solver.
  • DenseSolver is exact and fast for small-medium problems; it leverages gaussx structural dispatch for operators like Kronecker, BlockDiag, and LowRankUpdate.
  • CGSolver and BBMMSolver are iterative solvers for large PSD systems. BBMMSolver also drives the shared mBCG pass of gaussx.inv_quad_logdet.
  • PreconditionedCGSolver dramatically improves CG convergence on noisy kernel matrices by using a low-rank Cholesky preconditioner.
  • LSMRSolver handles rectangular and ill-conditioned systems that other PSD-only solvers cannot.
  • ComposedSolver decouples solve and logdet: pair any solve strategy with any logdet strategy for maximum flexibility.
  • AutoSolver removes the need to choose: it inspects operator type and size and delegates to the appropriate backend.

n_inducing = 12


def rbf(x1, x2, ls, var):
    return var * jnp.exp(-0.5 * (x1[:, None] - x2[None, :]) ** 2 / ls**2)


def build_sparse_gp(x_data, x_inducing, ls, var, noise):
    """Build the sparse GP covariance as a LowRankUpdate."""
    # K_XI  (N, N_I)
    kernel_data_inducing = rbf(x_data, x_inducing, ls, var)
    # K_II  (N_I, N_I)
    kernel_inducing = rbf(x_inducing, x_inducing, ls, var)

    # Nystrom: U = K_XI L_IIᵀ⁻¹ with L_II L_IIᵀ = K_II
    jitter = 1e-5 * jnp.eye(len(x_inducing))
    chol_inducing = jnp.linalg.cholesky(kernel_inducing + jitter)
    nystrom_factor = jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(
        chol_inducing, kernel_data_inducing.T, lower=True
    ).T

    # Σ_y = σ_ε² I + U Uᵀ
    return gaussx.low_rank_plus_diag(noise * jnp.ones(len(x_data)), nystrom_factor)


# Initial setup
x_inducing = jnp.linspace(-3.5, 3.5, n_inducing)
ls, var, noise = 1.0, 1.0, noise_std**2

sigma = build_sparse_gp(x_data, x_inducing, ls, var, noise)

def elbo(log_params, x_data, y_data, x_inducing):
    ls = jnp.exp(log_params[0])
    var = jnp.exp(log_params[1])
    noise = jnp.exp(log_params[2])

    sigma_op = build_sparse_gp(x_data, x_inducing, ls, var, noise)

    # Log-likelihood term
    # α = Σ_y⁻¹ y
    alpha = gaussx.solve(sigma_op, y_data)
    # −½ yᵀ α
    data_fit = -0.5 * jnp.dot(y_data, alpha)
    # −½ log det Σ_y
    complexity = -0.5 * gaussx.logdet(sigma_op)
    # −(N/2) log 2π
    const = -0.5 * len(y_data) * jnp.log(2 * jnp.pi)

    # Trace correction: tr(K_XX − Q_XX) / (2 σ_ε²)
    # K_XX diagonal = σ_k² (for RBF with same point)
    # Q_XX diagonal = diag(U Uᵀ)
    q_diag = jnp.sum(sigma_op.U**2, axis=1)
    # −(1 / 2σ_ε²) tr(K_XX − Q_XX)
    trace_correction = -0.5 * jnp.sum(var - q_diag) / noise

    return data_fit + complexity + const + trace_correction


log_params = jnp.log(jnp.array([ls, var, noise]))
print(f"Initial ELBO: {elbo(log_params, x_data, y_data, x_inducing):.2f}")

docs.title: Sparse Variational GP with Inducing Points¶
docs.text:
Sparse GPs approximate the full kernel with $N_{\mathcal{I}} \ll N$ inducing points:

$$\mathbf{K}_{XX} \approx \mathbf{K}_{X\mathcal{I}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}X}$$

The resulting covariance is $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top$ — a LowRankUpdate in gaussx. We optimize the ELBO with respect to inducing point locations and kernel hyperparameters via jax.grad.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
Sparse GP methods address the $O(N^3)$ cost of exact GP inference by introducing $N_{\mathcal{I}} \ll N$ inducing inputs $\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{I}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathcal{I}} \times D_x}$. The key idea is to approximate the full GP posterior via a variational distribution that conditions on the inducing values $\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{I}} = f(\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{I}})$. The Nystrom approximation gives:

$$\mathbf{K}_{XX} \approx \mathbf{Q}_{XX} = \mathbf{K}_{X\mathcal{I}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}X}$$

The variational free energy (VFE) framework (Titsias, 2009) optimizes a lower bound on the log-marginal likelihood:

$$\mathrm{ELBO}_\text{VFE} = \log \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_{XX} + \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I}) - \frac{1}{2 \sigma_\varepsilon^2} \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{K}_{XX} - \mathbf{Q}_{XX})$$

The trace correction penalizes the approximation error, and the bound is tight when the inducing points explain all the data.

docs.title: Build Nystrom approximation¶
docs.text: The Nystrom factor $\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{K}_{X\mathcal{I}} \mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N_{\mathcal{I}}}$ gives $\mathbf{Q}_{XX} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top$, so the noisy covariance $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top$ is a rank-$N_{\mathcal{I}}$ update of a diagonal -- exactly a LowRankUpdate. This is why gaussx can apply the Woodbury identity for $O(N N_{\mathcal{I}}^2 + N_{\mathcal{I}}^3)$ solve and the matrix determinant lemma for $O(N N_{\mathcal{I}}^2 + N_{\mathcal{I}}^3)$ logdet.

docs.title: ELBO (variational lower bound)¶
docs.text:
$$\mathrm{ELBO} = \log \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y}; \mathbf{0}, \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top) - \frac{1}{2 \sigma_\varepsilon^2} \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{K}_{XX} - \mathbf{Q}_{XX})$$

The first term uses gaussx solve + logdet. The trace correction penalizes information lost by the approximation.

docs.text: Component gaussx role low_rank_plus_diag Build Nystrom covariance gaussx.solve Woodbury solve for weights gaussx.logdet Matrix determinant lemma for ELBO jax.grad Differentiate through everything

def sparse_gp_lml(y, sigma_op):
    """Sparse GP log-marginal likelihood."""
    # α = Σ_y⁻¹ y
    alpha = gaussx.solve(sigma_op, y)
    # −½ yᵀ α
    data_fit = -0.5 * jnp.dot(y, alpha)
    # −½ log det Σ_y
    complexity = -0.5 * gaussx.logdet(sigma_op)
    # −(N/2) log 2π
    constant = -0.5 * len(y) * jnp.log(2 * jnp.pi)
    return data_fit + complexity + constant

docs.title: Structured GP: Kronecker and Low-Rank¶
docs.text:
This notebook shows where gaussx shines: exploiting structure in kernel matrices for Gaussian process inference.

We cover two common patterns:

  1. Kronecker structure — GP on a grid (e.g. spatial data on a regular mesh)
  2. Low-rank + diagonal — sparse GP with inducing points (Nystrom approximation)

The two most common forms of kernel structure in GP models are (1) Kronecker products from separable kernels on grids, and (2) low-rank approximations from inducing point methods. Both reduce the $O(N^3)$ cost of dense GP inference. gaussx supports both through its operator type system, dispatching to the optimal algorithm automatically.

docs.title: Part 1: Kronecker GP on a grid¶
docs.text:
When input data lies on a grid, the kernel matrix factorizes as a Kronecker product: $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{K}_1 \otimes \mathbf{K}_2$. This turns $O(N^3)$ operations into $O(N_1^3 + N_2^3)$ where $N = N_1 N_2$.

For a separable kernel on 2D inputs the factorization is:

$$k(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}') = k_1(s_1, s_1') k_2(s_2, s_2')$$

This includes products of any 1D stationary kernels (e.g. RBF, Matern). See Saatci (2012) for a comprehensive treatment of Kronecker methods in GP models.

docs.title: Kronecker logdet¶
docs.text:
The key identity: $\log \det (\mathbf{K}_1 \otimes \mathbf{K}_2) = N_2 \log \det \mathbf{K}_1 + N_1 \log \det \mathbf{K}_2$

gaussx computes this automatically — no need to form the $N \times N$ matrix.

docs.title: Kronecker solve and Cholesky¶
docs.text: Solve and Cholesky also decompose per-factor.

docs.title: Part 2: Low-rank GP (Nystrom / inducing points)¶
docs.text:
For non-grid data, a common approximation is $\mathbf{K}_{XX} \approx \mathbf{K}_{X\mathcal{I}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}X}$. The resulting covariance is $\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_\varepsilon^2) + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top$ — a low-rank update.

The Woodbury identity gives an efficient solve:

$$(\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top)^{-1} = \sigma_\varepsilon^{-2} \mathbf{I} - \sigma_\varepsilon^{-2} \mathbf{U} (\mathbf{I} + \sigma_\varepsilon^{-2} \mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U})^{-1} \mathbf{U}^\top \sigma_\varepsilon^{-2}$$

and the matrix determinant lemma gives an efficient logdet:

$$\log \det (\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top) = N \log \sigma_\varepsilon^2 + \log \det (\mathbf{I} + \sigma_\varepsilon^{-2} \mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U})$$

Both reduce the cost from $O(N^3)$ to $O(N N_{\mathcal{I}}^2 + N_{\mathcal{I}}^3)$, with $\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N_{\mathcal{I}}}$ and $N_{\mathcal{I}}$ the number of inducing inputs.

docs.title: Setup: random 1D data with inducing points¶
Construct gaussx LowRankUpdate operator¶
docs.text: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top$

docs.title: Solve and logdet via Woodbury¶
docs.text: gaussx automatically uses the Woodbury identity for solve and the matrix determinant lemma for logdet — O(nk^2 + k^3) instead of O(n^3).

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Structure When to use Solve cost Logdet cost Kronecker(K1, K2) Grid data O(n1^3 + n2^3) O(n1^3 + n2^3) low_rank_plus_diag Inducing points O(nk^2 + k^3) O(nk^2 + k^3) Dense Unstructured O(n^3) O(n^3)

gaussx dispatches to the right algorithm automatically based on the operator type — write the math once, get efficient computation for free.

docs.text:

  • Saatci, Y. (2012). Scalable Inference for Structured Gaussian Process Models. PhD thesis, University of Cambridge.
  • Rasmussen, C. E. & Williams, C. K. I. (2006). Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning. MIT Press.

def neg_lml(log_lengthscale, log_noise_variance, inputs, obs):
    lengthscale = jnp.exp(log_lengthscale)
    noise_variance = jnp.exp(log_noise_variance)
    difference = inputs[:, None] - inputs[None, :]
    # Σ_y = K_XX + σ_ε² I
    obs_covariance = jnp.exp(-0.5 * difference**2 / lengthscale**2)
    obs_covariance = obs_covariance + noise_variance * jnp.eye(len(obs))
    operator = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(obs_covariance, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
    return -gaussx.log_marginal_likelihood(jnp.zeros_like(obs), operator, obs)

cholesky_factor = jnp.linalg.cholesky(covariance)
cholesky_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(cholesky_factor)

# Whitened parameters (identity covariance in whitened space)
whitened_covariance_op = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(
    jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((N,), jnp.float64)
)

# Unwhiten covariance: L I Lᵀ = L Lᵀ = Σ
recovered_covariance = gaussx.whiten_covariance(cholesky_op, whitened_covariance_op)
print(
    "max error (covariance):",
    jnp.max(jnp.abs(recovered_covariance.as_matrix() - covariance)),
)

# Unwhiten a sample: z ~ 𝒩(0, I), x = L z ~ 𝒩(0, Σ)
key, sample_key = jax.random.split(key)
whitened_sample = jax.random.normal(sample_key, (N,))
unwhitened_sample = gaussx.unwhiten(whitened_sample, cholesky_op)
unwhitened_manual = cholesky_factor @ whitened_sample
print("max error (sample):", jnp.max(jnp.abs(unwhitened_sample - unwhitened_manual)))

# Verify empirically: many samples through L should have covariance ~ Σ
key, empirical_key = jax.random.split(key)
whitened_samples = jax.random.normal(empirical_key, (10_000, N))
# each row is L zᵢ
samples = whitened_samples @ cholesky_factor.T
empirical_covariance = jnp.cov(samples.T)
print(
    "mean abs error (empirical cov):",
    jnp.mean(jnp.abs(empirical_covariance - covariance)),
)

docs.title: Sugar Operations for Gaussians and GPs¶
docs.text:
gaussx provides "sugar" functions that combine primitives (solve, logdet, trace, etc.) into compound operations common in Gaussian and GP workflows.

What you'll learn:

  1. quadratic_form and gaussian_log_prob for evaluating distributions
  2. gaussian_entropy and kl_standard_normal for information-theoretic quantities
  3. log_marginal_likelihood for GP model selection
  4. schur_complement and cov_transform for conditional distributions
  5. whiten_covariance and unwhiten for reparameterization

These compound operations appear repeatedly in GP inference (Rasmussen & Williams, 2006), variational inference (Blei et al., 2017), and Bayesian neural networks. gaussx sugar functions combine primitives into numerically stable implementations — for example, log_marginal_likelihood avoids separate computation of the quadratic form and logdet, which can be more efficient with certain solver strategies.

docs.title: 1. Setup¶
docs.text: We build a small PSD kernel matrix from an RBF kernel on 20 points and wrap it as a lineax operator.

docs.title: 2. Quadratic forms¶
docs.text: quadratic_form(Sigma_op, x) computes $\mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{x}$ via a single solve -- the squared Mahalanobis distance.

docs.title: 3. Log-probability¶
docs.text:
gaussian_log_prob(mu, Sigma_op, x) evaluates the multivariate normal log-pdf:

$$\log \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = -\frac{1}{2} (N \log 2\pi + \log \det \boldsymbol{\Sigma} + (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}))$$

docs.title: 4. Entropy and KL divergence¶
docs.text:
Entropy of $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$:

$$\mathbb{H}[\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})] = \frac{1}{2} (N (1 + \log 2\pi) + \log \det \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$$

KL to the standard normal $\mathrm{KL}[\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \Vert \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})]$:

$$\mathrm{KL}[\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \Vert \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})] = \frac{1}{2} (\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) + \boldsymbol{\mu}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu} - N - \log \det \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$$

docs.title: 5. GP log-marginal likelihood¶
docs.text:
For GP regression with observations $\mathbf{y}$, prior mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_y$, and covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y = \mathbf{K}_{XX} + \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I}$:

$$\log p(\mathbf{y}) = -\frac{1}{2} ((\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_y)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y^{-1} (\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_y) + \log \det \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y + N \log 2\pi)$$

docs.title: 6. Schur complement¶
docs.text:
For GP conditional distributions, the Schur complement gives the conditional covariance:

$$\mathbf{K}_{X \mid Z} = \mathbf{K}_{XX} - \mathbf{K}_{XZ} \mathbf{K}_{ZZ}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{ZX}$$

schur_complement returns a LowRankUpdate operator that preserves the low-rank structure.

The Schur complement is the key identity behind GP conditional distributions. Given the joint $\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{f}_X \\ \mathbf{f}_Z \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{K}_{XX} & \mathbf{K}_{XZ} \\ \mathbf{K}_{ZX} & \mathbf{K}_{ZZ} \end{pmatrix}\right)$, the conditional $\mathbf{f}_X \mid \mathbf{f}_Z$ has covariance $\mathbf{K}_{XX} - \mathbf{K}_{XZ} \mathbf{K}_{ZZ}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{ZX}$. When $M \ll N$, this is a rank-$M$ correction — exactly a LowRankUpdate.

docs.title: 7. Covariance propagation¶
docs.text: cov_transform(J, Sigma_op) propagates uncertainty through a linear map: $\mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{J}^\top$ with $\mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$.

docs.title: 8. Whitening and unwhitening¶
docs.text:
The reparameterization trick for Gaussians: sample $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, then compute $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{z}$ to get $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ where $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{L}^\top$.

whiten_covariance(L, S_tilde) computes $\mathbf{L} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z \mathbf{L}^\top$, and unwhiten(m_tilde, L) computes $\mathbf{L} \boldsymbol{\mu}_z$.

The reparameterization trick (Kingma & Welling, 2014) enables gradient-based optimization of variational objectives by expressing samples $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{z} + \boldsymbol{\mu}$ where $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, making the sampling differentiable w.r.t. the distribution parameters $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\mathbf{L}$.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
This notebook demonstrated the main gaussx sugar operations:

Function What it computes quadratic_form $\mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{x}$ (Mahalanobis distance squared) gaussian_log_prob Multivariate normal log-pdf gaussian_entropy $\mathbb{H}[\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})]$ kl_standard_normal $\mathrm{KL}[\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \Vert \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})]$ log_marginal_likelihood GP log evidence (differentiable) schur_complement $\mathbf{K}_{XX} - \mathbf{K}_{XZ} \mathbf{K}_{ZZ}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{ZX}$ as LowRankUpdate cov_transform $\mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{J}^\top$ (uncertainty propagation) whiten_covariance / unwhiten Reparameterization trick

All operations dispatch on operator structure (diagonal, Kronecker, block-diagonal, low-rank) for efficient computation, and compose seamlessly with jax.jit, jax.vmap, and jax.grad.

docs.title: References¶
docs.text:
• Blei, D. M., Kucukelbir, A., & McAuliffe, J. D. (2017). Variational inference: a review for statisticians. JASA, 112(518), 859-877.
  • Kingma, D. P. & Welling, M. (2014). Auto-encoding variational Bayes. Proc. ICLR.
  • Rasmussen, C. E. & Williams, C. K. I. (2006). Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning. MIT Press.

variance = 1.0


def rbf_kernel(x1, x2):
    """Scalar RBF kernel: (D,), (D,) -> scalar."""
    sq_dist = jnp.sum((x1 - x2) ** 2)
    return variance * jnp.exp(-0.5 * sq_dist / lengthscale**2)


# Build the kernel matrix Σ_y = K_XX + σ_ε² I
def kernel_matrix(X):
    """Compute the full kernel matrix for training points."""
    n = X.shape[0]
    kernel = jax.vmap(lambda x1: jax.vmap(lambda x2: rbf_kernel(x1, x2))(X))(X)
    return kernel + noise_var * jnp.eye(n)

noisy_kernel_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(noisy_kernel, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)

# Σ_y⁻¹ operator (needed for predictive variance)

    jnp.linalg.inv(noisy_kernel), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)

        rbf_kernel, x_dyn, alpha_dyn, noisy_kernel_dyn_inv, state_t, integrator

        jnp.atleast_2d(var_t + dynamics_noise), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
    )

docs.title: GP with Uncertain Inputs (PILCO-style)¶
docs.text:
When a Gaussian process (GP) is queried at an uncertain input $\mathbf{x}_* \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$, the predictive distribution $p(f(\mathbf{x}_*))$ is no longer Gaussian -- it is a mixture of Gaussians weighted by the input density. Approximating this distribution is central to several important models:

  • Multi-step dynamics prediction (Girard et al., 2003): the GP predicts the next state, and that uncertain prediction becomes the input for the following step. Uncertainty compounds.
  • PILCO (Deisenroth & Rasmussen, 2011): a GP dynamics model is rolled forward under a policy, and the expected cost is differentiated through the uncertain predictions to learn the policy.
  • Bayesian GPLVM (Titsias & Lawrence, 2010): latent inputs are uncertain, so the likelihood requires integrating the GP over the variational posterior of the inputs.
  • Heteroscedastic / input-noise GPs (McHutchon & Rasmussen, 2011): noisy inputs induce effective output noise that depends on the local gradient of the GP mean.

docs.title: Predictive moments¶
docs.text:
Given the GP posterior $f \mid \mathcal{D}$ with weights $\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y^{-1} \mathbf{y}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y = \mathbf{K}_{XX} + \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I}$, and an uncertain input $\mathbf{x}_* \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$, the predictive moments are

$$\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x}_*)] = \int \mathbf{k}_{X*}^\top \boldsymbol{\alpha} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_*; \boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_*,$$

$$\mathbb{V}[f(\mathbf{x}_*)] = \int \left(f(\mathbf{x}_*) - \mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x}_*)]\right)^2 \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_*; \boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_*.$$

For the squared-exponential kernel, these integrals have closed-form solutions. For general kernels, we need numerical integration -- and that is where gaussx's uncertainty propagation machinery comes in.

docs.title: What this notebook covers¶
docs.text:
1. Training a 1D GP on $\sin(x)$ data
  2. Single uncertain prediction with Taylor, Unscented, and MC methods
  3. Multi-step dynamics rollout (PILCO-style) with growing uncertainty
  4. Expected cost computation under input uncertainty
  5. Expectation utilities: mean, gradient, and log-likelihood expectations
  6. AssumedDensityFilter diagnostics: skewness, kurtosis, Gaussianity

docs.title: 1. Setup: 1D GP regression on sin(x)¶
docs.text: We train a standard GP with an RBF kernel on noisy observations of $\sin(x)$, then extract the weight vector $\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y^{-1} \mathbf{y}$ and the inverse kernel operator $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y^{-1}$.

docs.title: 2. Single uncertain prediction¶
docs.text: Now suppose our test input is uncertain: $x_* \sim \mathcal{N}(1.5, 0.3)$. We compare three approaches to computing the predictive moments $\mathbb{E}[f(x_*)]$ and $\mathbb{V}[f(x_*)]$.

docs.title: 2d. Comparison¶
docs.text: All three methods should broadly agree, with Taylor slightly biased in regions of high curvature and MC showing some sampling noise.

docs.title: 3. Multi-step dynamics prediction (PILCO-style)¶
docs.text:
This is the core idea behind PILCO: chain uncertain GP predictions to roll out a trajectory. At each step, the output distribution becomes the input for the next step, and uncertainty grows.

We use a simple 1D dynamical system: $x_{t+1} = \sin(x_t) + 0.1 x_t + \varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01)$.

docs.title: Roll out with uncertainty propagation¶
docs.text: Starting from $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0.5, 0.01)$, we chain uncertain GP predictions for $T = 15$ steps. At each step we use AssumedDensityFilter for KL-optimal Gaussian moment matching.

docs.title: Plot: predicted trajectory vs ground truth¶
4. Expected cost under input uncertainty¶
docs.text: In PILCO, the policy is optimised by differentiating the expected cumulative cost through the uncertain rollout. Here we compute the expected quadratic cost at a single step.

docs.title: 5. Expectation utilities¶
docs.text: gaussx provides several utilities for computing expectations under Gaussian distributions. These are the building blocks for the uncertain GP machinery above.

docs.title: 5a. Mean expectation: $\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x})]$¶
docs.text: Compute the expected value of a function under a Gaussian input.

docs.title: 5b. Gradient expectation: $\mathbb{E}[\nabla f(\mathbf{x})]$ via Stein's lemma¶
docs.text:
Stein's lemma states that for $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$:

$$\mathbb{E}[\nabla f(\mathbf{x})] = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x^{-1} \mathrm{Cov}[\mathbf{x}, f(\mathbf{x})]$$

This is useful for computing expected gradients without differentiating through the expectation integral.

docs.title: 5c. Log-likelihood expectation: $\mathbb{E}[\log p(y \mid f(\mathbf{x}))]$¶
docs.text: For variational inference and EM with uncertain inputs, we need the expected log-likelihood under the input distribution.

docs.title: 6. AssumedDensityFilter with diagnostics¶
docs.text: The AssumedDensityFilter projects the true (non-Gaussian) output distribution onto the closest Gaussian in KL divergence. This is the workhorse behind multi-step rollouts. The integrate_with_diagnostics method additionally returns skewness and kurtosis of the output samples, which helps assess whether the Gaussian approximation is reasonable.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Tool Purpose uncertain_gp_predict Uncertain-input GP via quadrature uncertain_gp_predict_mc GP prediction with uncertain inputs via Monte Carlo AssumedDensityFilter KL-optimal Gaussian projection with diagnostics mean_expectation $\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x})]$ under Gaussian input gradient_expectation $\mathbb{E}[\nabla f(\mathbf{x})]$ via Stein's lemma cost_expectation Expected cost under input uncertainty log_likelihood_expectation $\mathbb{E}[\log p(y \mid f(\mathbf{x}))]$

These building blocks compose naturally:

  1. Train a GP dynamics model on observed transitions
  2. Roll out uncertain predictions with uncertain_gp_predict
  3. Evaluate expected cost with cost_expectation
  4. Differentiate through the whole pipeline with jax.grad

This is the computational recipe behind PILCO and related model-based reinforcement learning algorithms.

    mean = float(result.state.mean[0])
    variance = float(result.state.cov.as_matrix()[0, 0])
    return mean, variance

docs.title: Uncertainty Propagation through Nonlinear Functions¶
docs.text: When a Gaussian random variable $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$ with $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ passes through a nonlinear function $f$, the output $\mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}$ is generally not Gaussian. Different methods approximate the output distribution $p(\mathbf{y})$ with varying fidelity.

docs.title: Motivation: uncertain inputs in Gaussian processes¶
docs.text:
The problem of propagating uncertainty through nonlinear maps arises naturally in Gaussian process (GP) models with uncertain inputs. At test time the input $\mathbf{x}_*$ may itself be uncertain — for example:

  • In multi-step-ahead prediction with GP dynamics models (Girard et al., 2003; Deisenroth & Rasmussen, 2011), the predicted state at time $t$ becomes the uncertain input at time $t+1$.
  • In GP-based policy search (PILCO; Deisenroth & Rasmussen, 2011), the controller must evaluate a GP whose input is a belief state.
  • In heteroscedastic and input-noise models (McHutchon & Rasmussen, 2011), observation noise in the inputs induces effective output noise that depends on the local gradient of the GP posterior mean.

Given a GP posterior $f \mid \mathcal{D}$ and an input distribution $\mathbf{x}_* \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$, we seek the predictive moments

$$\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x}_*)] = \int f(\mathbf{x}) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}$$

$$\mathbb{V}[f(\mathbf{x}_*)] = \int (f(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x}_*)])^2 \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}$$

For the squared-exponential kernel these integrals have analytic forms (Quinonero-Candela et al., 2003), but for general kernels or composed models they are intractable — and the methods compared below become essential.

docs.title: Methods compared¶
docs.text:
This notebook compares six approaches available in gaussx:

Method Points Key idea Taylor 1st 1 (mean only) Linearize $f$ at the mean Taylor 2nd 1 + Hessian Add curvature correction (mean only) Taylor 2nd (var) 1 + Hessian Curvature correction (mean + variance) Unscented $2D_x+1$ sigma points Deterministic quadrature Monte Carlo $N_{\mathcal{E}}$ random samples Empirical moments Pure MC $N_{\mathcal{E}}$ random samples Direct histogram (ground truth)

We propagate a 1-D Gaussian through a deliberately wiggly function to expose how each method handles nonlinearity.

docs.title: The nonlinear function¶
docs.text:
We pick a function with an inflection point, asymmetry, and saturation -- features that challenge linearisation-based methods:

$$f(x) = \sin(1.5 x) \exp(-0.15 x^2) + 0.3 x$$

docs.title: Input distribution¶
docs.text:
A 1-D Gaussian ($D_x = D_y = 1$) centred right where the function has strong curvature:

$$x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_x = 1.0, \sigma_x^2 = 0.6)$$

docs.title: Mathematical background¶
docs.text: All methods below approximate the first two moments of $\mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{x})$ when $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$, as $\boldsymbol{\mu}_y \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_y}$.

docs.title: Taylor 1st order (linearisation / EKF)¶
docs.text:
Expand $f$ to first order around the mean, with Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_f \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_x}$:

$$f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x) + \mathbf{J}_f (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_x), \quad \mathbf{J}_f = \left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right|_{\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_x}$$

Under this linear approximation the output is exactly Gaussian:

$$\boldsymbol{\mu}_y = f(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x)$$

$$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y = \mathbf{J}_f \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x \mathbf{J}_f^\top$$

This is the update used in the extended Kalman filter (EKF) (Anderson & Moore, 1979). It is exact when $f$ is affine, but ignores curvature — the mean estimate is biased whenever $f''(\mu_x) \neq 0$ in one dimension.

docs.title: Taylor 2nd order¶
docs.text:
Including the second-order term of the Taylor expansion gives a correction to the mean via the Hessian $ abla^2 f_i( oldsymbol{\mu}_x) \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x imes D_x}$ of output component $i$:

$$\mu_{y,i} = f_i( oldsymbol{\mu}_x) + rac{1}{2} \mathrm{tr}( abla^2 f_i( oldsymbol{\mu}_x) oldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$$

With correct_variance=False, the covariance remains the first-order expression $ oldsymbol{\Sigma}_y = \mathbf{J}_f oldsymbol{\Sigma}_x \mathbf{J}_f^ op$ — this "second-order EKF" (mean-only correction) appears in Athans et al. (1968).

By default (correct_variance=True), the covariance also receives a second-order correction using fourth Gaussian moments:

$$[ oldsymbol{\Sigma}_y]_{ij} = [\mathbf{J}_f oldsymbol{\Sigma}_x \mathbf{J}_f^ op]_{ij} + rac{1}{2} \mathrm{tr}( abla^2 f_i( oldsymbol{\mu}_x) oldsymbol{\Sigma}_x abla^2 f_j( oldsymbol{\mu}_x) oldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$$

This can improve accuracy for mildly nonlinear functions but may overshoot for strongly nonlinear ones.

docs.title: Unscented transform (UT)¶
docs.text:
Instead of differentiating $f$, the UT (Julier & Uhlmann, 1997) evaluates it at a minimal set of sigma points $\{\boldsymbol{\chi}_i\}_{i=0}^{2D_x}$ chosen to match the mean and covariance of $\mathbf{x}$ exactly:

$$\boldsymbol{\chi}_0 = \boldsymbol{\mu}_x$$

$$\boldsymbol{\chi}_d = \boldsymbol{\mu}_x + \sqrt{D_x + \lambda} \mathbf{S}_d, \quad \boldsymbol{\chi}_{D_x + d} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_x - \sqrt{D_x + \lambda} \mathbf{S}_d$$

where $\mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^\top = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x$, $\mathbf{S}_d$ is the $d$-th column of the matrix square root $\mathbf{S}$ for $d = 1, \ldots, D_x$, and $\lambda = \alpha^2 (D_x + \kappa) - D_x$. The output moments are weighted sums, with mean weights $w_{m,i}$ and covariance weights $w_{c,i}$:

$$\boldsymbol{\mu}_y = \sum_{i=0}^{2D_x} w_{m,i} f(\boldsymbol{\chi}_i)$$

$$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y = \sum_{i=0}^{2D_x} w_{c,i} (f(\boldsymbol{\chi}_i) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_y) (f(\boldsymbol{\chi}_i) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_y)^\top$$

The UT captures nonlinear effects up to third order for Gaussian inputs (Julier & Uhlmann, 2004) and requires no derivatives of $f$. It underpins the unscented Kalman filter (UKF) (Wan & van der Merwe, 2000).

docs.title: Monte Carlo moment matching¶
docs.text:
Draw $N_{\mathcal{E}}$ members $\mathbf{x}^{(e)} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$ for $e \in \mathcal{E}$, push them through $f$, and compute empirical moments:

$$\boldsymbol{\mu}_y \approx \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} f(\mathbf{x}^{(e)})$$

$$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y \approx \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} (f(\mathbf{x}^{(e)}) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_y) (f(\mathbf{x}^{(e)}) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_y)^\top$$

This is unbiased and converges at rate $O(1/\sqrt{N_{\mathcal{E}}})$ regardless of dimension — making it the method of choice when $D_x$ is large or $f$ is very nonlinear. The moment-matched Gaussian is the best Gaussian approximation in the KL sense and is used for "assumed density filtering" in GP dynamics models (Deisenroth & Rasmussen, 2011).

docs.title: Visualisation¶
docs.text:
The main plot shows:

  • Bottom x-axis: the input Gaussian $p(x)$ as a filled curve.
  • Left y-axis: the nonlinear function $f(x)$ (black curve).
  • Right side: the output Gaussian approximations from each method, and the true output histogram from pure MC.

This makes it easy to see how the input bell curve "warps" through $f$ and how each approximation captures (or misses) the resulting skew.

docs.title: Observations¶
docs.text:
1. Taylor 1st order uses only the local slope at $\mu_x$ -- it produces a symmetric Gaussian whose width depends on $|f'(\mu_x)|$. When $f$ curves strongly, this misses the mean shift.

  2. Taylor 2nd order adds a Hessian correction to the mean ($\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{tr}(\nabla^2 f_i(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$) and gets closer to the true mean, but the covariance is still first-order.

  3. Taylor 2nd (var) additionally corrects the covariance using fourth Gaussian moments. For this wiggly function the correction overshoots — a common failure mode for strongly nonlinear functions.

  4. Unscented transform evaluates $f$ at $2D_x+1=3$ deterministic sigma points and captures the nonlinearity much better -- even with just 3 function evaluations.

  5. Monte Carlo (moment matching) converges to the true moments with enough samples. With 50k samples, the mean and variance match the pure MC histogram closely.

  6. The pure MC histogram reveals that the true output distribution is slightly skewed -- something no Gaussian approximation can capture. All four methods project onto the best-fit Gaussian, which is the optimal thing to do for downstream linear-Gaussian inference (Kalman updates, variational inference, etc.).

docs.title: When to use each method¶
docs.text:
Method Cost Best for Taylor 1st $O(D_x^2)$ Jacobian Mildly nonlinear, real-time EKF Taylor 2nd $O(D_x^3)$ Hessian Moderate nonlinearity, small $D_x$ Unscented $O(D_x)$ function evals Good default; no derivatives needed Monte Carlo $O(N_{\mathcal{E}})$ function evals Complex functions, large $D_x$, reference

All four methods are available in gaussx via the AbstractIntegrator interface, so you can swap them with a single line change:

integrator = gaussx.TaylorIntegrator(order=1)    # or
integrator = gaussx.UnscentedIntegrator()         # or
integrator = gaussx.MonteCarloIntegrator(n_samples=10000, key=jr.key(0))

result = integrator.integrate(f, state)

docs.title: Connection to GP prediction with uncertain inputs¶
docs.text:
In a trained GP with posterior mean $m(\mathbf{x})$ and variance $v(\mathbf{x})$, the total predictive variance under input uncertainty decomposes as (Girard et al., 2003, Eq. 2.40):

$$\mathbb{V}[y_*] = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_*}[v(\mathbf{x}_*)]}_{\text{noise / model variance}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{V}_{\mathbf{x}_*}[m(\mathbf{x}_*)]}_{\text{input uncertainty}}$$

The first term averages the GP's own uncertainty over plausible inputs; the second is exactly the output variance computed by the methods above, applied to the posterior mean function $m$.

For the squared-exponential (RBF) kernel, both expectations can be evaluated in closed form because the required Gaussian-times-kernel integrals are themselves Gaussian (Quinonero-Candela et al., 2003; Deisenroth, 2010, Appendix A). For other kernels (Matern, periodic, neural-network, etc.) or for compositions of GPs (deep GPs), the integrals are intractable and the numerical methods in this notebook are the standard approach.

The PILCO algorithm (Deisenroth & Rasmussen, 2011) chains these moment-matching steps across a planning horizon $T$ to perform gradient-based policy search in continuous state spaces, using the analytic RBF moments where possible and falling back to the unscented transform for the policy mapping.

lengthscale = 0.8

def rbf_kernel(x1, x2, ls=lengthscale, var=variance):
    """Squared-exponential kernel."""
    sq_dist = jnp.sum((x1[..., None] - x2[None, ...]) ** 2)
    return var * jnp.exp(-0.5 * sq_dist / ls**2)


def rbf_matrix(xa, xb, ls=lengthscale, var=variance):
    """Kernel matrix between two 1D input arrays."""
    sqdist = (xa[:, None] - xb[None, :]) ** 2
    return var * jnp.exp(-0.5 * sqdist / ls**2)

def unwhitened_elbo(
    mean_inducing,
    chol_inducing,
    y,
    kernel_inducing_op,
    kernel_data_inducing,
    kernel_diag,
    noise_var,
):
    """ELBO for the standard (unwhitened) SVGP."""
    # Σ_ℐ = L_ℐ L_ℐᵀ  (N_ℐ, N_ℐ)
    cov_inducing = chol_inducing @ chol_inducing.T
    cov_inducing_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(cov_inducing)

    # --- Predictive mean and variance via manual Nystrom ---
    # α = K_ℐℐ⁻¹ μ_ℐ  (N_ℐ,)
    alpha = lx.linear_solve(kernel_inducing_op, mean_inducing).value
    # μ_n = [K_Xℐ α]_n  (N,)
    f_loc = kernel_data_inducing @ alpha

    # Predictive variance: K_XX − K_Xℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹ K_ℐX + K_Xℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹ Σ_ℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹ K_ℐX
    # Solve K_ℐℐ @ W_col = K_ℐX_col for each column (data point)
    kernel_inducing_data = kernel_data_inducing.T  # (N_ℐ, N)
    _solve_col = lambda col: lx.linear_solve(kernel_inducing_op, col).value
    # W = K_ℐℐ⁻¹ K_ℐX  (N_ℐ, N)
    solved_cross = jax.vmap(_solve_col, in_axes=1, out_axes=1)(kernel_inducing_data)
    # σ²_n = [K_XX]_nn − [Wᵀ K_ℐX]_nn + [Wᵀ Σ_ℐ W]_nn  (N,)
    f_var = (
        kernel_diag
        - jnp.sum(solved_cross * kernel_inducing_data, axis=0)
        + jnp.sum(solved_cross * (cov_inducing @ solved_cross), axis=0)
    )

    # --- KL[q(f_ℐ) ‖ p(f_ℐ)] with p(f_ℐ) = 𝒩(0, K_ℐℐ) ---
    prior_loc = jnp.zeros(mean_inducing.shape[0])
    kl = gaussx.gaussian_kl(
        mean_inducing, cov_inducing_op, prior_loc, kernel_inducing_op
    )

    # --- ELBO ---
    return gaussx.variational_elbo_gaussian(y, f_loc, f_var, noise_var, kl)
def unwhitened_elbo( mean_inducing, chol_inducing, y, kernel_inducing_op, kernel_data_inducing, kernel_diag, noise_var, ): """ELBO for the standard (unwhitened) SVGP.""" # Σ_ℐ = L_ℐ L_ℐᵀ (N_ℐ, N_ℐ) cov_inducing = chol_inducing @ chol_inducing.T cov_inducing_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(cov_inducing) # --- Predictive mean and variance via manual Nystrom --- # α = K_ℐℐ⁻¹ μ_ℐ (N_ℐ,) alpha = lx.linear_solve(kernel_inducing_op, mean_inducing).value # μ_n = [K_Xℐ α]_n (N,) f_loc = kernel_data_inducing @ alpha # Predictive variance: K_XX − K_Xℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹ K_ℐX + K_Xℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹ Σ_ℐ K_ℐℐ⁻¹ K_ℐX # Solve K_ℐℐ @ W_col = K_ℐX_col for each column (data point) kernel_inducing_data = kernel_data_inducing.T # (N_ℐ, N) _solve_col = lambda col: lx.linear_solve(kernel_inducing_op, col).value # W = K_ℐℐ⁻¹ K_ℐX (N_ℐ, N) solved_cross = jax.vmap(_solve_col, in_axes=1, out_axes=1)(kernel_inducing_data) # σ²_n = [K_XX]_nn − [Wᵀ K_ℐX]_nn + [Wᵀ Σ_ℐ W]_nn (N,) f_var = ( kernel_diag - jnp.sum(solved_cross * kernel_inducing_data, axis=0) + jnp.sum(solved_cross * (cov_inducing @ solved_cross), axis=0) ) # --- KL[q(f_ℐ) ‖ p(f_ℐ)] with p(f_ℐ) = 𝒩(0, K_ℐℐ) --- prior_loc = jnp.zeros(mean_inducing.shape[0]) kl = gaussx.gaussian_kl( mean_inducing, cov_inducing_op, prior_loc, kernel_inducing_op ) # --- ELBO --- return gaussx.variational_elbo_gaussian(y, f_loc, f_var, noise_var, kl) In [6]: Copied! 
# Initialize variational parameters
m_init = jnp.zeros(M)
S_chol_init = jnp.eye(M)


@eqx.filter_jit
def unwhitened_step(mean_inducing, chol_inducing, lr=0.005):
    """One gradient ascent step on the unwhitened ELBO."""
    loss_fn = lambda m_, Sc_: (
        -unwhitened_elbo(
            m_,
            Sc_,
            y_train,
            kernel_inducing_op,
            kernel_data_inducing_train,
            kernel_diag_train,
            noise_var,
        )
    )
    loss, grads = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn, argnums=(0, 1))(
        mean_inducing, chol_inducing
    )
    # Clip gradients for stability
    g_m = jnp.clip(grads[0], -10.0, 10.0)
    g_S = jnp.clip(grads[1], -10.0, 10.0)
    m_new = mean_inducing - lr * g_m
    S_chol_new = chol_inducing - lr * g_S
    return m_new, S_chol_new, loss


m_uw, S_chol_uw = m_init.copy(), S_chol_init.copy()
losses_uw = []
for _i in range(300):
    m_uw, S_chol_uw, loss = unwhitened_step(m_uw, S_chol_uw)
    losses_uw.append(float(loss))

print(f"Unwhitened ELBO (final): {-losses_uw[-1]:.4f}")

def whitened_elbo(
    u_mean,
    u_chol,
    kernel_inducing_op,
    kernel_data_inducing,
    kernel_diag,
    y,
    noise_var,
):
    """ELBO for the whitened SVGP."""
    f_loc, f_var = gaussx.whitened_svgp_predict(
        kernel_inducing_op, kernel_data_inducing, u_mean, u_chol, kernel_diag
    )

    # Whitened KL: KL[𝒩(μ_z, Σ_z) ‖ 𝒩(0, I)]
    M_ = u_mean.shape[0]
    # Σ_z = L_z L_zᵀ  (N_ℐ, N_ℐ)
    S_w = u_chol @ u_chol.T
    # ½ (‖μ_z‖₂² + tr Σ_z − log det Σ_z − N_ℐ)
    kl = 0.5 * (jnp.sum(u_mean**2) + jnp.trace(S_w) - jnp.linalg.slogdet(S_w)[1] - M_)

    return gaussx.variational_elbo_gaussian(y, f_loc, f_var, noise_var, kl)
def whitened_elbo( u_mean, u_chol, kernel_inducing_op, kernel_data_inducing, kernel_diag, y, noise_var, ): """ELBO for the whitened SVGP.""" f_loc, f_var = gaussx.whitened_svgp_predict( kernel_inducing_op, kernel_data_inducing, u_mean, u_chol, kernel_diag ) # Whitened KL: KL[𝒩(μ_z, Σ_z) ‖ 𝒩(0, I)] M_ = u_mean.shape[0] # Σ_z = L_z L_zᵀ (N_ℐ, N_ℐ) S_w = u_chol @ u_chol.T # ½ (‖μ_z‖₂² + tr Σ_z − log det Σ_z − N_ℐ) kl = 0.5 * (jnp.sum(u_mean**2) + jnp.trace(S_w) - jnp.linalg.slogdet(S_w)[1] - M_) return gaussx.variational_elbo_gaussian(y, f_loc, f_var, noise_var, kl) In [8]: Copied! 
u_mean_init = jnp.zeros(M)
u_chol_init = jnp.eye(M)


@eqx.filter_jit
def whitened_step(u_mean, u_chol, lr=0.005):
    """One gradient ascent step on the whitened ELBO."""
    loss_fn = lambda um, uc: (
        -whitened_elbo(
            um,
            uc,
            kernel_inducing_op,
            kernel_data_inducing_train,
            kernel_diag_train,
            y_train,
            noise_var,
        )
    )
    loss, grads = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn, argnums=(0, 1))(u_mean, u_chol)
    g_um = jnp.clip(grads[0], -10.0, 10.0)
    g_uc = jnp.clip(grads[1], -10.0, 10.0)
    um_new = u_mean - lr * g_um
    uc_new = u_chol - lr * g_uc
    return um_new, uc_new, loss


u_mean_w, u_chol_w = u_mean_init.copy(), u_chol_init.copy()
losses_w = []
for _i in range(300):
    u_mean_w, u_chol_w, loss = whitened_step(u_mean_w, u_chol_w)
    losses_w.append(float(loss))

print(f"Whitened ELBO (final): {-losses_w[-1]:.4f}")

# --- Feature extractor: simple 2-layer MLP ---
d_features = 20

k_nn1, k_nn2 = jax.random.split(k3)
W1 = 0.5 * jax.random.normal(k_nn1, (1, 32))
W2 = 0.3 * jax.random.normal(k_nn2, (32, d_features))


def phi(x, W1=W1, W2=W2):
    """Feature extractor: x (N,) -> Phi (N, d_features)."""
    h = jnp.tanh(x[:, None] @ W1)  # (N, 32)
    return jnp.tanh(h @ W2)  # (N, d_features)


Phi_train = phi(x_train)
Phi_plot = phi(x_plot)
# --- Feature extractor: simple 2-layer MLP --- d_features = 20 k_nn1, k_nn2 = jax.random.split(k3) W1 = 0.5 * jax.random.normal(k_nn1, (1, 32)) W2 = 0.3 * jax.random.normal(k_nn2, (32, d_features)) def phi(x, W1=W1, W2=W2): """Feature extractor: x (N,) -> Phi (N, d_features).""" h = jnp.tanh(x[:, None] @ W1) # (N, 32) return jnp.tanh(h @ W2) # (N, d_features) Phi_train = phi(x_train) Phi_plot = phi(x_plot) In [12]: Copied! 
# Initialize natural parameters (prior: N(0, I))
nat1 = jnp.zeros(d_features)
nat2 = -0.5 * jnp.eye(d_features)

lr_blr = 0.8

for _step in range(20):
    # Current mean from natural params
    mu = jnp.linalg.solve(-2.0 * nat2, nat1)
    f_pred = Phi_train @ mu
    residual = y_train - f_pred

    # Gradient and Hessian of the log-joint, prior included
    grad = Phi_train.T @ residual / noise_var - mu  # (d,)
    # (d, d), negative definite
    hessian = -Phi_train.T @ Phi_train / noise_var - jnp.eye(d_features)

    nat1, nat2 = gaussx.blr_full_update(nat1, nat2, grad, hessian, lr_blr)

mu_blr_full = jnp.linalg.solve(-2.0 * nat2, nat1)
Sigma_blr_full = jnp.linalg.inv(-2.0 * nat2)

f_blr_full = Phi_plot @ mu_blr_full
f_blr_full_var = jnp.sum(Phi_plot * (Phi_plot @ Sigma_blr_full), axis=1)

print(f"BLR full-rank posterior mean norm: {jnp.linalg.norm(mu_blr_full):.4f}")

# The diagonal ignores the correlation between features, so a large step
# diverges here: it needs a small step and more of them than the full-rank case.
lr_blr_diag = 0.1

for _step in range(200):
    mu_d = nat1_diag / (-2.0 * nat2_diag)
    f_pred_d = Phi_train @ mu_d
    residual_d = y_train - f_pred_d

    grad_d = Phi_train.T @ residual_d / noise_var - mu_d
    hessian_diag_d = -jnp.sum(Phi_train**2, axis=0) / noise_var - 1.0

    nat1_diag, nat2_diag = gaussx.blr_diag_update(
        nat1_diag, nat2_diag, grad_d, hessian_diag_d, lr_blr_diag
    )

docs.title: Whitened SVGP & Bayesian Linear Regression¶
docs.text:
This notebook demonstrates the whitened parameterization for sparse variational GPs and its connection to Bayesian linear regression (BLR) in the "last-layer" GP setting. We cover:

  1. Standard (unwhitened) SVGP with the Titsias ELBO
  2. Whitened SVGP for improved optimization geometry
  3. The variance adjustment operator $\mathbf{Q}$
  4. BLR natural-parameter updates (full and diagonal)
  5. GGN and Hutchinson diagonal Hessian approximations
  6. Comparative plots

docs.title: 1. Background: Whitened Parameterization¶
docs.text:
In a standard SVGP we place a variational distribution $q(\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{I}}) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{I}}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathcal{I}})$ over the inducing values $\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{I}} = f(\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{I}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathcal{I}}}$. The KL divergence against the prior $p(\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{I}}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}})$ involves $\mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1}$ and $\log \det \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}$, which couples the variational parameters to the kernel hyperparameters and makes optimization hard.

The whitened reparameterization introduces $\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{I}} = \mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1} \mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{I}}$ where $\mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}$ is the Cholesky factor of $\mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}$. We parameterize:

$$q(\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{I}}) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_z, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z)$$

so that the induced distribution over $\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{I}}$ is:

$$q(\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{I}}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}} \boldsymbol{\mu}_z, \mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z \mathbf{L}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^\top)$$

The prior in whitened space is simply $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, so the KL divergence simplifies to:

$$\mathrm{KL}[q(\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{I}}) \Vert p(\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{I}})] = \frac{1}{2} \left( \Vert \boldsymbol{\mu}_z \Vert_2^2 + \mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z) - \log \det \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z - N_{\mathcal{I}} \right)$$

This decouples the variational parameters from the kernel hyperparameters and yields better-conditioned gradients.

docs.title: 3. Kernel Matrices¶
docs.text: We use an RBF kernel throughout. All covariance matrices are wrapped as lineax operators so they plug directly into gaussx primitives.

docs.title: 4. Standard (Unwhitened) SVGP¶
docs.text: We initialize $q(\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{I}}) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{I}}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathcal{I}})$ with $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{I}} = \mathbf{0}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathcal{I}} = \mathbf{I}$, then optimize the ELBO.

docs.title: 5. Whitened SVGP¶
docs.text: Now we use the whitened parameterization. The variational parameters are $\boldsymbol{\mu}_z$ (whitened mean) and $\mathbf{L}_z$ (Cholesky of whitened covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z = \mathbf{L}_z \mathbf{L}_z^\top$). The predictive distribution is computed by whitened_svgp_predict.

docs.title: 6. SVGP Variance Adjustment¶
docs.text:
The operator $\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathcal{I}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1} - \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1}$ appears in the predictive variance of any SVGP:

$$\mathbb{V}[f_*] = k_{**} + \mathbf{k}_{*\mathcal{I}} \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{k}_{\mathcal{I}*}$$

svgp_variance_adjustment builds this operator lazily.

docs.title: 7. BLR Connection: "Last-Layer" GP¶
docs.text:
A GP with random Fourier features (RFF) or a neural-network feature extractor $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\phi}$ reduces to Bayesian linear regression in the feature space. The posterior over the weights $\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\phi}$ is maintained in natural parameters $(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_\theta \boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta, -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_\theta)$ where:

  • $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_\theta \boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1} \boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta$
  • $-\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_\theta = -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\theta^{-1}$

Updates use the gradient and Hessian of the log-joint: the Gaussian log-likelihood plus the prior $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$. The prior keeps the precision invertible, since these features are strongly correlated.

docs.title: 7a. Full-Rank BLR Update¶
docs.text:
blr_full_update performs a damped natural-parameter update with step size $\gamma$, gradient $\mathbf{g}$ and Hessian $ abla^2_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}$ of the log-joint:

$$- rac{1}{2} oldsymbol{\Lambda}_ heta^ ext{new} = (1 - \gamma) \left(- rac{1}{2} oldsymbol{\Lambda}_ heta ight) + \gamma \left( rac{1}{2} abla^2_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} ight)$$

$$( oldsymbol{\Lambda}_ heta oldsymbol{\mu}_ heta)^ ext{new} = (1 - \gamma) oldsymbol{\Lambda}_ heta oldsymbol{\mu}_ heta + \gamma \left(\mathbf{g} - abla^2_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} oldsymbol{\mu}_ heta ight)$$

docs.title: 7b. Diagonal BLR Update¶
docs.text: blr_diag_update is the diagonal counterpart where $-\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_\theta$ is stored as a vector (diagonal entries only).

docs.title: 8. GGN Diagonal¶
docs.text: The Generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix $\mathbf{J}^\top \mathbf{J}$ approximates the Hessian of the loss with respect to network parameters. Its diagonal is cheap to compute and useful for diagonal Laplace or diagonal natural gradient updates.

docs.title: 9. Hutchinson Hessian Diagonal¶
docs.text:
When the Hessian is only accessible via Hessian-vector products (HVPs), we can estimate its diagonal stochastically using the Hutchinson identity:

$$\mathrm{diag}(\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{v} \odot (\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathbf{v})]$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is a Rademacher random vector.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Primitive Purpose whitened_svgp_predict Predictive mean and variance in whitened space svgp_variance_adjustment Build the $\mathbf{Q}$ operator for predictive variance trace_correction Titsias trace penalty variational_elbo_gaussian Closed-form ELBO for Gaussian likelihoods gaussian_kl General KL between two multivariate normals blr_full_update Full-rank natural-parameter BLR step blr_diag_update Diagonal natural-parameter BLR step ggn_diagonal Diagonal of $\mathbf{J}^\top \mathbf{J}$ (GGN approximation) hutchinson_hessian_diag Stochastic Hessian diagonal via Hutchinson

Key takeaways:

  • The whitened parameterization decouples variational parameters from kernel hyperparameters, giving faster and more stable convergence.
  • svgp_variance_adjustment encapsulates the algebraic bookkeeping of $\mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathcal{I}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1} - \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{I}}^{-1}$ behind a lazy operator.
  • Full-rank BLR in natural parameters converges in very few steps for Gaussian likelihoods. The diagonal version ignores correlations between features, so it needs a smaller step and many more iterations.
  • The GGN diagonal is exact and cheap; the Hutchinson estimator trades accuracy for the ability to work with implicit HVP access only.

docs.title: Woodbury Solve Step by Step¶
docs.text:
The Woodbury matrix identity turns an $N \times N$ solve into a cheap $k \times k$ solve when the matrix has low-rank structure:

$$(\mathbf{A}_0 + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{D} \mathbf{V}^\top)^{-1} = \mathbf{A}_0^{-1} - \mathbf{A}_0^{-1} \mathbf{U} \mathbf{C}^{-1} \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{A}_0^{-1}$$

where $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{D}^{-1} + \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{A}_0^{-1} \mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}$ is the capacitance matrix, $\mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}$ and $\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}$.

This notebook walks through each step and shows that gaussx.solve does it automatically.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
The Woodbury identity (also known as the matrix inversion lemma or Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula) is one of the most important identities in computational linear algebra. It appears in:

  • Sparse GP inference — the Nystrom approximation yields a low-rank + diagonal covariance, and the Woodbury identity turns the $N \times N$ inversion into a $k \times k$ problem where $k \ll N$.
  • Kalman filtering — sequential rank-1 updates to the state covariance are applied via the matrix inversion lemma at each time step.
  • Online learning — rank-1 covariance updates (e.g. recursive least squares) use the Sherman-Morrison special case.
  • Ridge regression with feature space formulations — the kernel trick relates the $N \times N$ and $D_x \times D_x$ solutions through Woodbury.

The identity was first published by Woodbury (1950) and independently by Sherman & Morrison (1950) for the rank-1 case.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: We construct $\mathbf{A} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{a}) + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{U}^\top$ where $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^{100}$ and $\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{100 \times 3}$ (rank 3).

docs.title: Matrix determinant lemma¶
docs.text:
Similarly, the logdet decomposes. This follows from the identity

$$\det (\mathbf{A}_0 + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{D} \mathbf{V}^\top) = \det (\mathbf{D}^{-1} + \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{A}_0^{-1} \mathbf{U}) \det \mathbf{D} \det \mathbf{A}_0$$

which is a direct consequence of the Schur complement determinant identity. Taking logarithms:

$$\log \det (\mathbf{A}_0 + \mathbf{U} \mathbf{D} \mathbf{V}^\top) = \log \det \mathbf{A}_0 + \log \det \mathbf{C} + \log \det \mathbf{D}$$

where $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{D}^{-1} + \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{A}_0^{-1} \mathbf{U}$ is the capacitance matrix. In our case ($\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{U}$):

docs.title: Cost comparison¶
docs.text:
Operation Dense Woodbury Solve $O(N^3)$ $O(Nk^2 + k^3)$ Logdet $O(N^3)$ $O(Nk^2 + k^3)$ Storage $O(N^2)$ $O(Nk)$

For $N = 100$ and $k = 3$, dense does about $10^6$ operations and Woodbury about 900.
